title: How ITC & DHL Support Small Businesses in Cross-Border Trade
content:
How ITC & DHL Support Small Businesses in Cross-Border Trade
Prioritise Us
on Google
The International Trade Centre (ITC) and DHL have signed a new memorandum of understanding to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Credit: Getty Images
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director of the International Trade Centre, says its DHL partnership will help SMEs overcome cross-border trade barriers
The International Trade Centre (ITC) and DHL have signed a new memorandum of understanding to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).
DHL and the ITC’s partnership dates back to 2016, with a focus on supporting
women-led businesses
in cross-border trades.
Through the renewed agreement, ITC’s market intelligence and trade expertise will be available to DHL’s global logistics network.
It aims to help SMEs overcome the barriers that continue to keep many of them out of international markets.
"For small businesses, the main challenge is not in creating quality products for customers but getting it to them," says Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director at ITC.
Key Facts: ITC-DHL Partnership Renewal
Partnership between ITC and DHL dates back to 2016
DHL GoTrade has reached more than 26,000 SMEs since 2021
ITC SheTrades has supported more than 4,000 women-led businesses
ecomConnect connected 400+ SMEs with DHL support between 2020-2024
Some markets saw shipping costs cut by up to 60% through the partnership
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director of ITC, and Hennie Heymans, CEO of DHL Express Sub-Saharan Africa, sign a Memorandum of Understanding renewing the ITC-DHL partnership. Credit: DHL Group
Inside the ITC-DHL trade partnership
Under the renewed agreement, ITC and DHL will support small businesses across exports,
supply chains and logistics
The partnership will work with business support organisations and ITC SheTrades Hubs to strengthen services for small and women-led companies.
SMEs and women entrepreneurs will also receive support in international trade discussions among private-sector and government bodies.
DHL says SMEs account for around 90% of businesses globally, provide roughly 70% of employment and contribute around 70% of global GDP.
Despite this, many continue to face barriers when attempting to fully participate in international trade.
Over the past decade, ITC and DHL have worked together through DHL GoTrade, ITC SheTrades and the ITC ecomConnect programme, reaching small businesses in more than 60
countries across Africa
, ASEAN, Latin America and the Caribbean.
Since 2021, GoTrade has supported more than 26,000 SMEs and 8,000 women-owned businesses.
EcomConnect linked more than 400 SMEs with DHL support between 2020 and 2024, including shipping arrangements that cut costs by up to 60% in some markets.
We're deepening our work with DHL to help more small businesses, particularly women-led businesses
Pamela Coke-Hamilton, Executive Director at ITC
Closing the SME finance gap
Logistics access is not the only barrier for SMEs trying to
trade internationally
, as access to finance remains a significant constraint.
The partnership specifically targets this issue for women-led businesses, as they traditionally face issues around funding.
According to the World Bank and International Finance Corporation's most recent MSME Finance Gap Report, SMEs across 119 emerging markets and developing economies face a combined financing shortfall of around US$5.7tn.
The report found that 40% of formal MSMEs are credit-constrained, with women-owned businesses alone accounting for approximately US$1.9tn of that gap.
Pamela says: “We're deepening our work with DHL to help more small businesses, particularly women-led businesses, to overcome
last-mile logistics
barriers and reach new markets and to ensure their perspectives are heard at decision-making tables.”
Initiatives like GoTrade and SheTrades represent a narrower, logistics-focused intervention within a far larger structural problem.
ITC and DHL’s agreement aims to address the financing gap, while reducing other obstacles standing between SMEs and the international markets.
Key companies
International Trade Centre
Executive Director: Pamela Coke-Hamilton
Headquarters: Geneva, Switzerland
The International Trade Centre is a joint agency of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation dedicated to supporting small and medium-sized enterprise competitiveness. It provides practical trade-led development solutions, market intelligence and sustainable technical assistance to help businesses in developing nations connect to global markets.
DHL Group
CEO: Tobias Meyer
Headquarters: Bonn, Germany
DHL Group is the world's leading express logistics and postal company, delivering global supply chain solutions, parcel delivery and international trade freight services. Driving connectivity across international markets, the organisation actively advances automated warehousing, digitised tracking networks and sustainable low-emission transport infrastructure.

title: ImportGenius: Turning Trade Data into Sourcing Intelligence

ImportGenius: Turning Trade Data into Sourcing Intelligence
Prioritise Us
on Google
ImportGenius is constantly working to improve visibility within the supply chain industry. Credit: ImportGenius
As the global trade environment becomes increasingly complex and more competitive, ImportGenius CEO Michael Kanko positions ImportGenius as a critical tool
Global supply chains are facing ongoing challenges and an increasingly competitive market.
As sustainability, speed and digitalisation increase in priorities – alongside
long-term resilience
– new organisations are emerging ready to fill the gap in the market.
In today’s world, choice is crucial, but it can be overwhelming for decision-makers.
Almost two decades ago, ImportGenius was founded in order to make global trade data transparent – now, it has expanded significantly and is working to revolutionise trade intelligence.
Organisation expansion
ImportGenius was founded in 2007, making headlines in 2008 when it discovered that
was preparing to launch the iPhone 3G. This occurred when it used its customs data to uncover 188 unrecorded containers that were shipped by Apple and its logistics partners.
Since then, the company has become a trusted data source for large-scale news outlets, has scaled its solutions to help global enterprises and has continuously expanded its operations into new markets.
Today, ImportGenius is working on transforming trade intelligence by using AI and other digital tools to enhance supply chain visibility. It collects, organises and makes information from the international trade industry accessible. Through this, it helps clients understand
shipping manifests
and customs records in order to make informed decisions with confidence.
It connects fragmented data and turns it into actionable information, helping readers find their ideal supplier, track market shifts and
navigate global trade
Key stats
3.3 billion+ shipments are recorded through ImportGenius
The company has insights into shipment-level records across more than 25 countries
ImportGenius has served more than 50K businesses
More than 8 million US importers are tracked
There is shipment data on more than 16 million importers and exporters around the world
ImportGenius can offer shipment-level insights into global trade (Credit: Getty Images)
Supply chain impact
In 2025, ImportGenius launched GlobalPro, its annual subscription service which offers enterprise-level access to US trade data, which is updated daily. This means there was more thorough visibility into global trade, faster time-to-value for sourcing and logistics teams and a greater depth of coverage.
As tariffs and
supply chain volatility
became a major concern for organisations in 2025, this service came at a crucial period. This level of insight into competitors and their international clients helped increase clarity for decision-makers. As new trade lanes were being established and cross-border strategies were becoming more complex, this data helped increase cohesion across data sets.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, 50% of US businesses close within five years, and 65% close within a decade.
ImportGenius CEO Michael Kanko points to a decline in competitiveness as a core reason. There are large numbers of competitors, but they lack the information to drive them into more innovative action.
ImportGenius, therefore, aims to increase this competitiveness by offering succinct data points about global supply chains. The increased level in transparency and cohesion helps drive business decisions and also influences wider
industry policy
We didn’t just create a tool: we created an entirely new way for businesses to see the world. Our data has changed supply chains, influenced policy and made businesses better and safer.
Founder & CEO of ImportGenius, Michael Kanko
Founder & CEO of ImportGenius, Michael Kanko. Credit: ImportGenius
ImportGenius, therefore, is helping organisations turn trade data into sourcing intelligence and supply chain analytics, offering shipment-level intelligence which provides strong market insights for supplier relationship management. Through this, clients can gain verified information on potential suppliers, market risk and sourcing opportunities.

HQ: California, US
Apple Inc. is a global technology leader headquartered in Cupertino, California, designing consumer electronics, software, and services worldwide. The company became ImportGenius's breakthrough case study in 2008 when trade data uncovered 188 unrecorded containers with the unreleased iPhone 3G. This discovery demonstrated customs intelligence power for competitive analysis, establishing ImportGenius as credible and proving shipping manifests reveal strategic insights before announcements.

The Association for Supply Chain Management (ASCM) is the global leader in supply chain education and certification. ASCM standards help professionals leverage intelligence platforms like ImportGenius to optimize sourcing decisions, manage supplier relationships, and build data-driven resilient supply chains.

title: CATL begins test production of battery cells in Debrecen - electrive.com
content:
Chinese battery giant CATL has begun test production of battery cells at its new plant in Debrecen, Hungary. Previously, there were multiple delays, forcing European automakers to source supplies from China as an alternative. More recently, political headwinds have also emerged.
Aerial view of the new CATL factory in Debrecen
Image: CATL
CATL has begun test production at its new battery cell plant in Debrecen, Hungary. According to the company, this follows the successful fulfilment of all necessary prerequisites and regulatory requirements. The test phase aims to fully set up, optimise, and validate the production facilities and manufacturing processes before mass production begins. The first two production lines at the plant have now been commissioned for these test purposes.
However, it remains unclear when full-scale mass production of battery cells in Debrecen will actually commence. Test production in new cell factories typically lasts months rather than weeks. On the other hand, CATL is the world’s largest battery cell manufacturer, with extensive experience in the field. Its customers are eagerly awaiting the cells: according to a media report, Mercedes-Benz
even had to halt
production of the all-electric GLC in Bremen this summer because CATL was unable to supply enough cells. In response, the company specifically restructured its supply chain to
temporarily supply Mercedes with cells from China
for the GLC and VLE.
CATL already operates a cell factory in Thuringia
CATL announced the Debrecen plant
in August 2022
as its second European cell factory, alongside the facility in Arnstadt, Thuringia, which opened at the end of 2022. The plan included investments of €7.34 billion and a production capacity of up to 100 GWh per year, making it CATL’s largest factory outside China. The Debrecen plant is set to supply locally produced cells to Mercedes-Benz, as well as BMW – which
also operates its new EV factory in Debrecen
– and other European automakers. Construction of the first phase began in 2023, but the originally expected production start was delayed several times; it was
supposed to begin in spring 2026
Additional challenges arose during the ramp-up, including approval and environmental issues. Local residents and environmental organisations contested the environmental permits, with experts criticising aspects such as water consumption, noise, and impacts on the water balance. This summer, a non-compliant wastewater discharge and elevated
nickel exposure among employees
led to regulatory interventions. While
production of battery modules had already begun
, cell manufacturing took longer to get underway.
The project also faces an increasingly critical political environment: the government of Viktor Orbán, which was voted out in April, had heavily supported Hungary’s development into a European battery hub and attracted several Asian manufacturers to the country. Following the change in government, the new leadership under Prime Minister Péter Magyar
announced stricter environmental controls and new oversight for the battery industry
. However, there is no clear evidence of a direct link between the political shift and the delays at CATL; the company emphasises that it has obtained the necessary approvals for the now-launched trial operation and has rectified the previously identified deficiencies.

title: 'Artificial' sounds fake: Trump renames AI 'super intelligence'
content: US President Donald Trump has announced that the US government will replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” in its documents, saying the word “artificial” makes intelligence sound fake.Trump made the announcement on Tuesday while addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York, days after asking the public to vote on alternative names for AI. He said the US would use “super intelligence” going forward and urged other countries to adopt the term.“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake, it makes it sound fake and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing,” Trump said during his UN address.The new name was not among the options in Trump’s original poll. On September 19, he had proposed Superior Intelligence, Extreme Intelligence and Supreme Intelligence as alternatives to artificial intelligence.From poll to governmentTrump’s renaming push comes as the US debates how quickly increasingly capable AI systems should be developed and whether additional safety measures are needed.In his UN speech, Trump dismissed warnings about the technology and said the US should not restrict its development. He described AI as a major technological transformation and linked leadership in the technology to global power.“Whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said, according to reporting on his UN address.Trump’s position follows a series of recent disputes over AI safety. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for measures to slow the development of frontier AI systems, arguing that rapidly advancing models could create serious risks. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has backed a federal framework for consistent safety requirements while arguing that companies can begin safety work without waiting for new legislation.Trump has instead characterized concerns about AI taking over or destroying humanity as a “hoax.” He has also said the US should support the technology rather than slow its growth.Why the name mattersThe phrase “super intelligence” already has a technical meaning in AI research. It generally refers to hypothetical AI systems whose capabilities exceed those of humans across a broad range of intellectual tasks.That makes Trump’s proposed terminology different from simply shortening artificial intelligence to a new acronym. The term he selected is already associated with a possible future stage of AI development rather than the broad range of systems currently described as AI.That future has also prompted warnings from researchers and executives working at some of the companies developing advanced AI systems. Jacob Coxon, who recently left Anthropic after previously working at OpenAI, warned that AI companies are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” He said people developing the technology “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger has similarly warned about the risks of future superintelligent systems. He wrote, “We really do earnestly believe A.I. could kill all humans!” and has argued that AI developers still lack a reliable way to ensure increasingly capable systems remain aligned with human interests.Paul Christiano, a former OpenAI alignment researcher and current board member of OpenAI’s nonprofit foundation, has also warned of a “meaningful risk” that AI could cause a “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control.” He has said the industry is not currently on track to reduce that risk to an acceptable level.Trump’s announcement also follows his creation of an “AI Force” and plans to appoint an AI “Czar.” He announced both measures on September 19 but did not initially provide detailed information about the structure or responsibilities of the proposed force.

title: 16 F-35 fighter jet simulators connected across four bases in drills
content: Lockheed Martin connected 16 F-35 full mission simulators across four military bases for a two-hour distributed mission rehearsal. The exercise also brought F-18 simulators and an E-2D Hawkeye controller into the same virtual mission from a fifth location.The event tested how crews stationed thousands of miles apart could coordinate during a simulated multidomain operation, the company said Monday. The participating sites maintained command-and-control links and completed every training objective during the exercise.Five bases connectedThe F-35 simulators operated from Marine Corps Air Stations Yuma, Miramar and Iwakuni, along with Naval Air Station Lemoore. The F-18 simulators and E-2D Hawkeye controller joined from Naval Air Station Oceana in Virginia.The arrangement allowed geographically separated crews and controllers to train together while working from their respective bases. Each team could operate within a common operational picture during the exercise.The setup also brought together U.S. Marine Corps and U.S. Navy units in a single training event. This gave participants experience coordinating with other platforms and units without moving aircraft or crews to one location.Air, surface and cyber operationsLockheed Martin used its tactical environment simulation to recreate a mission involving air, surface, and cyber operations. The scenario required participants to coordinate their actions while responding within the shared virtual environment.The exercise focused on maintaining communication and situational awareness as information moved between the participating locations. Command-and-control links remained active throughout the event, according to Lockheed Martin.Teams reported uninterrupted situational awareness and data exchange. The company said it completed every planned training objective during the two-hour rehearsal.“This exercise enabled warfighters to train the way they fight,” said Ken Garrett, vice president of F-35 Training and Logistics. “They complete complex missions in coordination across distances – their training should represent their missions.”Training across distancesThe exercise gave units based at separate installations a chance to rehearse coordination over long distances. Such training can help crews practice working with other units before taking part in live operations.The distributed format also allows participating forces to remain at their home bases during a joint rehearsal. That can support training between units that are separated by large geographic distances.The event showed how simulator networks can connect different aircraft and command platforms during the same mission. It also demonstrated the ability of participating teams to maintain a shared picture throughout the exercise.Building mission readinessThe successful rehearsal adds to Lockheed Martin’s work on distributed training for the F-35. Connecting simulators at multiple installations gives military units another way to prepare for missions that require coordination across locations.“Mission rehearsal across multiple bases builds the readiness, interoperability and confidence required to win tomorrow’s missions,” Garrett added.For forces operating from different regions, networked exercises can provide opportunities to train together without bringing aircraft to a common base. The latest event showed that geographically separated crews could complete a shared mission while maintaining communication and situational awareness throughout the exercise.

title: CATL starts trial run at its new 100 GWh EV battery plant
content: CATL has begun trial production of battery cells at its new factory in Debrecen, Hungary, marking a key step toward supplying European automakers from a local manufacturing base. The Chinese battery maker said on September 22 that the plant had secured the permits and met the regulatory requirements needed to start trial operations.The first two production lines are now being tested as CATL prepares the facility for series production. The company has not provided a date for full-scale manufacturing.First cell lines enter trial operationsTrial production will allow CATL to set up, optimize, and validate the equipment and manufacturing processes before series production begins. The company said the Debrecen facility had met all conditions required to begin the trial run.The firm received the plant’s occupancy permit in August 2026. It then obtained the remaining relevant permits and completed the requirements under its Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control (IPPC) permit.Local authorities carried out regular inspections before granting the occupancy permit. The inspections followed up on earlier issues that had caused concerns among local residents. Authorities confirmed that the deficiencies identified during the permitting process had been addressed.Factory targets European automakersCATL announced the Debrecen project in August 2022 as its second European battery plant after its facility in Germany. The company said the project is intended to strengthen its position in Europe’s automotive and electric mobility supply chain.Construction of the first cell building began in summer 2023, while production equipment installation was completed by spring 2026. The factory reportedly uses flexible production lines designed to meet the requirements of its customers.The facility has already been producing battery modules since autumn 2024. The battery maker said it has produced 537,000 modules at the Hungarian site so far.100 GWh capacity plannedOnce all planned facilities are ready, the Debrecen site is expected to become CATL’s largest manufacturing base outside China. The company has put its planned capacity at 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh).The factory is positioned near Hungary’s growing electric vehicle manufacturing sector. CATL said it will supply major European automakers that have established significant EV production capacity in the country.The start of cell trials comes after an earlier target for production. According to reports in September 2025, CATL’s European general manager Matt Shen informed that the company had been aiming to start production in late 2025 or early 2026.CATL steps up European battery productionThe firm said it will continue working with the Hungarian government and regulatory authorities throughout the trial period. The company will monitor employee health, safety, and environmental indicators and proactively submit the results to regulators.CATL is the world’s largest EV battery maker by installations. Data from South Korean market researcher SNE Research showed that the battery maker recorded 289.6 GWh of global battery installations from January through July 2026, up 26.6 percent from the same period a year earlier.Its global market share increased to 39.9 percent during the period, compared with 38.0 percent a year earlier. The Debrecen plant adds another major manufacturing location as CATL expands its production footprint closer to European vehicle manufacturers.

title: China integrates 50MW sCO2 plant with 100MW molten salt storage
content: Keep aside lithium-ion battery banks for a moment. China is banking on molten-salt storage and super-pressurized gas to keep its power grid stable as demand rises.Construction is reportedly underway on the Ruitan demonstration project at Shandong’s Bajiao power station. It is said to be the world’s first utility-scale facility combining supercritical carbon dioxide power generation with molten salt thermal energy storage.The facility is expected to be operational next year. It integrates a 50-megawatt supercritical carbon dioxide power generation unit with a 100-megawatt, 400 megawatt-hour molten salt energy storage system. Power grids are volatile, fickle things. When factories power down at midnight, standard coal plants waste vast amounts of energy just to stay spun up.The Ruitan facility operates like a thermal vault. During periods of low demand, the facility converts surplus power from coal units into stored heat using molten salt. When peak demand strikes, this stored heat powers a supercritical carbon dioxide unit to generate efficient electricity and maintain grid stability.sCO2 units are water-free, more compact, highly efficient, lower in carbon emissions, and can adjust load four times faster than coal units.China’s next big energy betCompared to standard power plants that boil water into steam to drive turbines, supercritical systems use carbon dioxide pressurized into a dense state with both gas and liquid properties. This fluid directly powers turbines inside a closed-loop system that requires zero water and runs with higher efficiency and lower carbon emissions. Interestingly, the technology offers four times the load-adjustment speed of conventional coal units and can draw heat from diverse sources like solar, geothermal, or industrial waste.The timing could not be better. While lithium-ion batteries dominate short-duration storage and mobile electronics, they degrade rapidly over an 8- to 10-year lifespan. On the other hand, molten salt tanks store energy reliably for over 30 years with virtually no capacity loss. Over several decades, that longevity slashes capital expenditure for long-duration grid storage.China is moving fast to establish a lead in the space. Guizhou province recently saw commercial operations launch at Chaotan One — the world’s first CO2 plant — which captures industrial waste heat from a local steel facility. Meanwhile, the China National Nuclear Corporation plans to roll out its own combined nuclear and molten-salt sCO2 system by 2028, and solar developers in Tibet are deploying molten-salt tanks at the 50-megawatt Dangxiong plant to store daytime solar energy.Higher efficiency & lower emissionsThe technology isn’t just a Chinese phenomenon. Projects like Europe’s SOLARSCO2OL are integrating similar loops into concentrated solar plants. Aerospace and nuclear researchers worldwide eye closed-loop sCO2 systems for next-generation reactors and spacecraft propulsion.Unlike chemical batteries suited for mobile devices, molten salt systems store excess energy as heat in large liquid salt tanks. Operators can use this thermal energy directly or convert it back into electricity. As a result, the Ruitan facility would give energy companies a practical way to meet strict decarbonization goals without tearing down existing infrastructure. Power producers can convert obsolete coal facilities into adaptable, water-free clean energy centers. These converted plants store massive amounts of thermal energy for weeks, stabilize power grids during demand spikes, and extend the operating life of valuable industrial sites for decades.

title: F-35 vs Ferrari: Italian Navy to soon settle a wild high-speed race
content: The Italian Navy is preparing for an unusual acceleration test. An F-35B fighter jet will race a Ferrari SF90 on a runway at the Navy’s air base in Grottaglie, southern Italy.The matchup is scheduled for October 11 and will pit one of the world’s most advanced short-takeoff and vertical-landing fighters against a road-going hybrid supercar. The event is designed to compare the two machines over short distances, before the F-35B takes to the air.Ferrari versus F-35BThe first race will cover 500 meters (1,640 feet) on an aluminum runway used by the Italian Navy’s F-35Bs for landing, Tom Kington from Defense News reported. Both machines will accelerate from a standing start, with the fighter expected to take longer to get moving but potentially make up ground as its power builds.Ferrari driver Fabio Barone, who has previously set seven speed records in Ferrari cars, will drive the SF90. He said the car normally accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h (0–62 mph) in 2.8 seconds, but modifications to its engine are expected to reduce that to about 2.6 seconds for the event.Barone expects the Ferrari to reach approximately 330 km/h (around 205 mph) during the 1,640-foot run and complete it in roughly eight to nine seconds. The driver also expects acceleration forces of around 2.2g during the run.The F-35B has a very different job. Rather than relying on wheels and a conventional drivetrain, it uses a Pratt & Whitney F135 turbofan and its short-takeoff and vertical-landing system to generate thrust. The aircraft is expected to start more slowly than the Ferrari but has considerably greater power available as it accelerates. At the end of the first 1,640 feet race, the F-35B will take off.The second race gets even strangerA second contest will combine a ground race with flight. The 2.8-kilometer (1.74-mile) course will use both asphalt and aluminum surfaces. The Ferrari and F-35B will initially accelerate side by side, but after the first 1,640 feet, the fighter will take off and continue the race in flight at about 20 meters (66 feet).According to Defense News, the two machines will share a runway about 35 meters (about 115 feet) wide, leaving roughly 15 meters (roughly 49 feet) between them during the ground portion of the race. For Barone, driving on the aluminum plates could be one of the biggest challenges. He expects the surface to generate more vibration than conventional asphalt.The event will therefore test two very different interpretations of acceleration. The Ferrari’s ability to rapidly convert engine power into forward motion through its tires, and the F-35B’s ability to turn enormous thrust into acceleration before transitioning into flight.A tradition of racing cars against fightersIn 2003, Formula One driver Michael Schumacher raced a Ferrari Formula One car against an Italian Air Force Eurofighter at Grosseto Air Base. The Eurofighter won the longer 900-meter (2,953-foot) and 1,200-meter (3,937-foot) races without taking off, while Schumacher won the 600-meter (1,969-foot) contest.Schumacher reached 294 km/h (183 mph) and completed the 600-meter (1,969-foot) run in 9.6 seconds, beating the fighter by two-tenths of a second. Barone has his own history with unusual aviation-related Ferrari runs. In 2025, he drove a Ferrari along the flight deck of the Italian Navy’s Trieste amphibious assault ship, reaching 164 km/h (102 mph) over approximately 200 meters (around 656 feet) before braking at the end of the deck.In October 2007, Lincolnshire, UK, Top Gear staged a unique two-mile drag race pitting presenter Richard Hammond in a 1,001-horsepower Bugatti Veyron against RAF Flight Lieutenant Jim Walls in a Eurofighter Typhoon jet. The rules required the car to sprint a mile down the runway and back, while the jet took off, climbed a mile vertically, and dived back down to the finish line. Despite the Veyron taking an early lead off the line, the Eurofighter Typhoon utilized its superior jet thrust to overtake the hypercar and claim a comfortable victory. The upcoming F-35B race continues that tradition, but with a modern fighter designed specifically to operate from short runways and ships. The result will ultimately depend on how the two machines are matched over each distance. A Ferrari may have the advantage during the first few seconds, while the F-35B’s enormous thrust becomes more useful as speed builds and the fighter has one ability its four-wheeled rival does not: it can simply leave the runway.

title: Nuclear waste could be buried for under 0.1 cent/kWh, US study finds
content: Deep boreholes could provide a safe and relatively low-cost way to permanently dispose of radioactive waste left after used nuclear fuel is recycled, according to results from a three-year US Department of Energy-funded project.Deep Isolation evaluated multiple disposal scenarios involving waste from recycled nuclear fuel. Its analysis found that every scenario studied was projected to cost less than the program’s target of 0.1 cent per kilowatt-hour of electricity generated.Long-term safety modeling also found that all scenarios under expected conditions met the study’s safety criteria. In most cases, projected radiation doses to the public were orders of magnitude below the 10 millirem-per-year regulatory benchmark used in the analysis.The research was conducted under the Department of Energy’s ARPA-E CURIE program with Argonne National Laboratory, Oklo and Case Western Reserve University. Deep Isolation was responsible for studying how recycling waste could be packaged and permanently isolated underground.Burying recycled nuclear wasteThe company’s approach uses deep boreholes drilled into geologically suitable rock formations. The project considered its Universal Canister System in both horizontal and vertical borehole configurations.Researchers examined the full disposal process, including the characteristics of waste produced during fuel recycling, how that material could be packaged, repository design, long-term safety and disposal economics.“This project shows the value of designing recycling and disposal systems together rather than treating waste management as a downstream consideration,” said Jesse Sloane, executive vice president of engineering at Deep Isolation.The work is designed to complement emerging approaches that aim to extract additional value from used nuclear fuel rather than treating all of it as waste.Oklo, one of the project partners, is developing a fuel strategy involving used-fuel recycling, fuel fabrication and power generation. Its planned process would use pyroprocessing to recover usable fuel materials, fabricate them into new fuel and use that fuel in advanced fast reactors.Even after recycling, however, radioactive material requiring permanent disposal remains. The CURIE project examined whether deep boreholes could provide that final disposal pathway without undermining the economics of recycling.Canisters link fuel cycleA key part of Deep Isolation’s approach is its Universal Canister System, or UCS. The triple-purpose system is being developed to handle spent fuel and high-level radioactive waste during storage, transportation and eventual disposal.The company says the design could accommodate waste streams from both existing and advanced reactors. The CURIE analysis considered how the canisters could be placed in either vertical or horizontal deep borehole repositories.“Closing the fuel cycle is about unlocking the full value of used nuclear fuel — recovering its energy potential and extracting isotopes, while safely and permanently managing what remains,” said Ed Petit de Mange, vice president of fuel recycling at Oklo.The findings could also inform the Department of Energy’s Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses, where fuel recycling is being explored alongside other parts of the nuclear fuel cycle.Deep Isolation is separately working toward real-world deployment of its technology. In January 2026, the company launched a full-scale, at-depth commercialization pilot in Cameron, Texas, aimed at demonstrating its deep-borehole disposal system.

title: Qnetic’s 200kWh Pulsar prototype enters low-speed testing phase
content: Flywheel-based energy storage system manufacturer Qnetic has reached an important milestone after it began low-speed testing of Pulsar, its 200kWh prototype system. The testing will validate the control and safety systems before moving onto higher rotational speeds. The rapid increase in renewable energy installations has also driven higher demand for energy storage systems. The intermittent nature of solar and wind energy systems makes them unfit to be connected to the grid directly, prompting the need for a reliable energy storage system. While lithium-ion batteries are the best solution that we have in terms of high storage capacities, they are also extremely expensive and have limited life cycles. Researchers have been looking for alternative approaches that can deliver the power densities of lithium-ion batteries at a fraction of the cost, while maintaining performance characteristics. Flywheel-based energy storage is a top contender for this spot as it offers low-cost and highly scalable options. How a flywheel energy storage system worksQnetic’s alternative to the lithium-ion battery consists of a flywheel, or a heavy rotor, capable of spinning at supersonic speed in a frictionless vacuum chamber. The energy generated at renewable energy power plants is used to accelerate the flywheel and store it as kinetic motion, instead of carrying out the chemical reactions in a lithium-ion battery. When electricity demand picks up, the rotor can be decelerated by connecting it to a generator that converts the kinetic motion into electric charge that can then be supplied to the grid on demand. Since the energy storage involves no chemical conversion, there is no risk of degradation of the rotor even after many years. Recently, Qnetic completed its first 100 continuous charge-discharge cycles with zero faults or degradation, a key indicator of its reliability. Additionally, the motor generated 130 kW of power output at 97.3 percent efficiency, with speeds over 11,000 rpm (revolutions per minute), validating the power conversion architecture of the system. Since the amount of energy stored in the system places high demands on the mechanical systems, controls, and containment in the system, Qnetic is using a staged validation program approach to validate the system. Independent validationThis milestone follows Pulsar’s mechanical assembly, completed in June, and multiple component and structural tests. These tests aim to reduce the system’s technical risk before it operates at full speed“Our approach is to increase operating conditions methodically, validating the data at each stage and resolving issues before moving on. That process fundamentally de-risks a system of this scale before full-speed testing and eventual customer deployment,” said Michael Pratt, CEO of Qnetic, in a press release. Results from Pulsar testing are also being shared with the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) as part of Readiness Informed by Shared Knowhow, Evaluation, and Data (deRISKED) program, where Qnetic is a participant. “Independent validation is a critical part of moving an emerging energy storage technology from development into the field,” added Pratt in the press release.“The data we’re generating with Pulsar allows us, EPRI, and ultimately utilities and customers to evaluate the technology based on measured performance. We’re deliberately building that evidence as we move toward commercialization.”

title: Quaise Energy to help US complete first geothermal energy development
content: A geothermal project under construction in central Oregon is aiming to generate more than 50 megawatts of electricity by 2030 by tapping heat far below the Earth’s surface. Its developer, Quaise Energy, says Project Obsidian could become the world’s first commercial superhot geothermal power plant.The company announced that the US Department of Energy has selected the project for up to $25 million in funding. The proposed contract would help Quaise study its first two wells and use the results to plan a third. Three wells to test the resourceProject Obsidian is being built south of Bend on a geothermal resource that Quaise says has been extensively studied. A confirmation well is currently being drilled at the site.The initial three-well configuration is designed to demonstrate more than 25 MW of gross electric capacity, with average reservoir temperatures exceeding 572°F. That figure describes the planned test. Quaise separately expects the project’s first phase to produce more than 50 MW by 2030, when it aims to deliver its first power to the Pacific Northwest grid.The DOE support would fund analysis of drilling, stimulation and flow results from the first two wells. Quaise plans to use those findings to optimize the third well and guide later drilling at the site.“This DOE support is a recognition of what we are building at Quaise and the progress we are making in the field, including the confirmation well currently being drilled at Project Obsidian,” said Carlos Araque, CEO and President of Quaise Energy. “Our ambition has always been to make superhot geothermal a commercial reality, and Project Obsidian is where we first deliver on that promise,” he added.Drilling toward hotter rockQuaise expects to drill a well reaching temperatures above 752°F at Project Obsidian, which it says would make it the hottest well in the Western Hemisphere. Those temperatures exceed the range of current commercial geothermal projects.The project uses enhanced geothermal systems, or EGS, and advanced drilling techniques to access heat in rock deep underground. Quaise says the approach could eventually make firm geothermal power available across a much wider range of locations.Results from the three wells would provide an early measure of whether the project can produce electricity at the planned scale. The DOE-funded work would also let Quaise and its research partners collect and share field data from drilling, stimulation, and flow testing.A larger project remains possibleQuaise says Project Obsidian has the potential to expand to up to 1 gigawatt of electric capacity. That is a possible future buildout, separate from both the three-well test and the first-phase target for 2030. The company has not detailed how many additional wells such an expansion would require.Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Oregon State University are part of the project team.The DOE selection follows Quaise’s close of $180 million in Series B financing in August 2026 to fund Project Obsidian. For now, the next milestone is the well work: gathering the data needed to assess the resource and plan the project’s next stage.

title: Scientists discover amoeba that can reproduce at scorching 145°F
content: A single-celled organism collected from a steaming creek in California can reproduce at temperatures that would stop any other known complex life form. Researchers discovered the amoeba in Lassen Volcanic National Park and found that it could divide at up to 145°F.The team named the new species Incendiamoeba cascadensis, or “fire amoeba of the Cascade mountain range.” Their findings raise the known temperature limit for reproduction in eukaryotes – the group that includes animals, plants, fungi, and amoebas.A discovery in a steaming creekSyracuse University microbiologist Angela Oliverio and her colleagues collected water from a geothermal tributary of Hot Springs Creek. In the lab, PhD student Beryl Rappaport examined the samples under a microscope and spotted a cell changing shape and moving through the water.“That’s definitely an amoeba. That’s characteristic amoeba movement,” she said. Rappaport used extra-long barbecue tongs to lower the sample vials into the steaming water.The team’s tests showed that the organism could reproduce at temperatures up to 145°F and remain active at up to 147°F. It also recovered after exposure to 158°F when returned to cooler conditions. Reproducing at 145°F and recovering from a hotter exposure are separate findings: the amoeba does not multiply at 158°F.Genetic analysis confirmed that the researchers had found a previously undescribed species.How does the fire amoeba handle heat?High temperatures can damage the proteins and membranes that cells need to function. By comparing the fire amoeba’s genome with those of other amoebas, the researchers identified features that may help it keep those cellular components stable.The result is striking because eukaryotes have more complex cell structures than bacteria and archaea, some of which live at or above water’s boiling point. Those organisms have long held the most extreme heat records, while the temperature limits of many microscopic eukaryotes remain poorly understood.“So few have been described, especially in detail. We have a lot to learn from them,” Rappaport said.The new species suggests that scientists may find other heat-tolerant eukaryotes by looking more closely at geothermal environments.What the discovery could meanFor Oliverio, the record matters because it shows that a previously assumed boundary can be crossed.“It wasn’t so much the incremental amount that this record was broken by, as much as the proof that it was possible,” she said.Understanding how the amoeba protects its cells could eventually inform research into temperature-stable medicines or heat-resilient crops. Those applications remain possibilities, however; the researchers have identified an organism with unusual abilities, not a ready-made way to transfer them to other species.The discovery also gives scientists another example to consider when asking where life might persist beyond Earth. For now, its clearest lesson comes from a small California creek: even among complex cells, researchers are still finding organisms that push the known limits of life.The findings were published in the journal Cell.

title: Scientists use 10-nm coating to extend anode-free EV battery life
content: South Korean researchers have developed a nanoscale electrode design that could help make electric-vehicle batteries smaller and lighter while extending their operating life. The technology uses semiconductor manufacturing techniques to address uneven lithium deposition, a major obstacle facing anode-free batteries.Anode-free batteries could potentially increase the amount of energy stored within a given battery size. However, their commercial development has been limited by unstable lithium deposits that reduce performance during repeated charging and discharging.Removing the conventional anodeStandard lithium-ion batteries contain an anode material, typically graphite, that stores lithium while the battery charges. Anode-free designs remove this material and instead deposit lithium directly onto a thin copper current collector.Eliminating graphite frees up space and reduces weight, potentially allowing manufacturers to build batteries with higher energy density. For electric vehicles, that could translate into lighter battery packs or greater driving range without increasing pack size.The design also creates a difficult engineering problem. Lithium does not always spread evenly across flat copper foil. Instead, it can accumulate in particular areas and develop into sharp, branching structures called dendrites.These formations destabilize the protective layer surrounding the lithium and encourage unwanted reactions with the electrolyte. Battery performance consequently declines rapidly over repeated cycles.Earlier attempts to solve the problem have included adding surplus lithium or placing thick protective coatings on the electrode. Although these measures can offset lithium losses or shield its surface, they also increase battery weight and volume.Microscopic tubes guide lithium depositionThe KAIST-led team modified the copper foil itself using secondary sputtering lithography, or SSL, a precision fabrication method associated with semiconductor manufacturing.Researchers created regularly spaced, tube-shaped structures measuring approximately 300 nanometers across and 150 nanometers high. The arrangement provides defined sites where lithium can settle, helping it spread across the electrode rather than accumulating in isolated areas.The microscopic structures increased the surface area available for lithium deposition to around four times that of untreated flat copper foil. This larger deposition area helped limit the concentrated lithium growth that can produce dendrites.The researchers compared the arrangement to marking closely spaced parking spaces across an otherwise open lot. Each structure helps direct the incoming lithium toward an available location.Ultrathin layer forms stronger protectionThe team also coated the structured copper foil with an MXene layer roughly 10 nanometers thick. MXenes are two-dimensional materials with surface properties that can be tailored for electrochemical applications.Instead of functioning as the final protective barrier, the coating behaves like a primer. In the study’s LiPF6-based electrolyte, its surface encouraged the development of a uniform protective layer rich in lithium fluoride.That layer reduced unwanted reactions between lithium and the electrolyte while further suppressing dendrite growth. The researchers examined its composition and formation using techniques including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry and transmission electron microscopy.“This study shows how ultrafine fabrication techniques used in semiconductor manufacturing can create both uniform sites for lithium deposition and a stable protective layer without changing the bulk electrolyte formulation or adding excess lithium,” Professor Jinwoo Lee said.The research findings were published online in Advanced Functional Materials on September 1.

title: US Army tests 30mm combat vehicle built to counter drone threats
content: BAE Systems has delivered two new AMPV 30 concept infantry fighting vehicles to the US Army, combining a 30mm remote turret with systems designed to detect drone threats and share targets across the battlefield.The vehicles were delivered in April for the Army’s Transformation in Contact (TiC) 2.0 initiative and have since undergone field evaluations, including live-fire testing. The program allows soldiers to test emerging technology under operational conditions and provide feedback on what works.BAE developed the two vehicles in just six months using $17 million of its own research and development funding. The design builds on the chassis of the company’s Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle, or AMPV.Rather than developing an entirely new combat vehicle, BAE modified the existing platform using its common top plate. The approach allows different weapons and mission equipment to be integrated onto the same underlying vehicle architecture.30mm turret boosts firepowerBoth AMPV 30 prototypes carry Kongsberg’s Medium Caliber Turret, a compact remote turret system that is already in production for the US Marine Corps’ Amphibious Combat Vehicle.The remotely operated turret allows soldiers to use the weapon system while remaining protected inside the armored vehicle. Its integration also demonstrates how the AMPV platform can be adapted for an infantry fighting vehicle role.“Our mission was speed and innovation, and we delivered beyond expectations,” said Bill Sheehy, vice president of BAE Systems’ Ground Maneuver futures.“With today’s battlefield evolving faster than ever, it’s paramount that Soldiers have the capabilities they need to win the fight. Throughout this effort, our team demonstrated how we can integrate new design solutions in a time-effective and more cost-efficient manner for the Army.”The prototypes add more than firepower. They are equipped with counter-unmanned aircraft system capabilities intended to help soldiers combat drone threats, an increasingly important requirement for armored vehicles.BAE has also added a cross-platform target handoff system. It allows multiple vehicles to connect and exchange targeting information, helping crews identify targets and coordinate their response across the battlefield.Crews see beyond armorA 360-degree situational awareness camera system gives soldiers a view of their surroundings without requiring them to leave the protection of the vehicle. Together, the sensors, connectivity and counter-drone systems are intended to improve crew awareness and survivability.The modular design is central to BAE’s approach. Its common top plate and the AMPV’s open architecture allow different mission equipment packages to be installed without redesigning the entire vehicle.According to BAE, the platform can accommodate more than 30 different turret systems. That gives the Army options to modify the vehicle’s weapons and equipment as operational requirements change.The two AMPV 30s bring the number of turreted AMPV prototypes funded by BAE over the past two years to eight. The latest vehicles are now being evaluated by soldiers to determine how the combination of firepower, counter-drone capability and battlefield connectivity performs under field conditions.

title: US Navy eyes 2 Virginia and 1 Columbia submarines yearly by 2031
content: The US Navy has announced a novel strategy to speed up its nuclear submarine construction, and will reportedly deliver three boats a year from 2031 in order to expand its undersea fleet.The strategy was outlined by Vice Adm. Robert Gaucher, the Navy’s Director of Submarine Programs. He is the Pentagon’s first-ever direct reporting portfolio manager (also called submarine czar), after officially taking office in early 2026.Gaucher detailed a four-pillar approach that’s set to increase the production of Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarines, and Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines. The Navy is reportedly targeting two Virginia-class and one Columbia-class submarine annually.According to the czar, the Navy aims to achieve that rate by 2031 or sooner. The strategy aims to expand the fleet while easing submarine production bottlenecks. “The Navy’s requirement to increase the submarine production rate to at least one Columbia-class and two Virginia-class submarines per year remains the top industrial base priority,” he said.Expanding the submarine fleetAccording to Naval News, the lead Columbia-class submarine, which is designed to replace the Ohio class, is expected to be delivered in 2028. Construction of the first vessel began on 1 October 2020. It is scheduled to enter service in 2031.The Navy aims to reach a production rate of one Columbia-class submarine per year by 2030. Production of Virginia-class submarines, intended to replace older Los Angeles-class attack submarines, is expected to reach two boats annually by 2031.In earlier testimony before the House Appropriations Defense Subcommittee on May 12, Adm. Daryl Caudle, the US Navy’s 34th Chief of Naval Operations, said the Navy expects to hit the higher production rate around 2032.The planned Columbia-class submarine.Credit: A total of 12 Columbia-class submarines are planned. At the same time, another 44 Virginia-class submarines are under construction or planned as part of an eventual 70-boat class.Both programs depend on the same industrial base. The submarines are made by General Dynamics Electric Boat in Connecticut, and Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia. “You can’t look at Virginia and Columbia in a vacuum because you’re sharing workforce, it’s the same shipyard, you’re sharing footprint,” Gauche explained. Fewer design changesThe first of Gaucher’s four-pillar strategy involves locking in submarine designs to prevent modifications from slowing construction. “We’re done with engineering churn,” he said. The czar has reportedly ordered a “pencils down” approach for the Virginia-class submarines. This means that any design changes will generally be avoided unless required for safety or critical operational reasons. This is set to become particularly important as production moves through the final Virginia-class variants, Blocks VII and VIII.The second pillar allows the main shipyards to focus on assembling submarines, installing equipment and carrying out final tests. The third pillar expands on this approach by increasing the capacity of the wider submarine industrial base.Finally, the last pillar looks beyond the Virginia class to the future SSN-X nuclear attack submarine. “At some point, if I could have two submarines instead of one submarine, that might be better than paying an exorbitant cost with money and time for the added capability,” Gaucher concluded.

title: US lab develops quantum sensor for chemical and biological threats
content: Scientists at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) are developing a quantum sensing platform that could eventually let warfighters detect chemical and biological threats with a device small enough to carry into the field.The system is designed to combine the broad detection capabilities of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy with the portability of a much smaller sensor. APL researchers envision a fieldable device roughly the size of a laptop that could analyze extremely small samples of potentially hazardous substances.Shrinking NMR with quantum sensorsNMR spectroscopy uses magnetic fields to manipulate the spins of atomic nuclei. The resulting signals contain information about the structure of molecules, allowing researchers to distinguish between different substances.The technique is already widely used in laboratories, but conventional NMR systems are difficult to take into the field. They typically require powerful superconducting magnets, cryogenic cooling equipment, and relatively large sample volumes.APL experimental physicist Isaiah Gray and his team are pursuing a different approach based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond.An NV center is created when a nitrogen atom replaces a carbon atom in a diamond and a neighboring carbon atom is missing. This creates a quantum system that responds to surrounding magnetic fields.When illuminated with green laser light, the NV center emits red light. By measuring that light, researchers can determine the NV center’s spin state and use it to infer information about nearby molecular structures.The approach can potentially work with samples containing only tens or hundreds of atoms, dramatically reducing the amount of material required compared with conventional NMR.The nano-container challengeThe concept is promising, but sensitivity remains a major obstacle. Nuclear spins at the diamond’s surface need to remain measurable for sufficient time to produce a useful signal. Gray’s team has proposed physically confining those spins in tiny structures, described by the researchers as “nano-containers,” fabricated directly on the diamond surface.Computer simulations indicate that one of the geometries studied by the team could improve NMR sensitivity and accuracy by roughly an order of magnitude. The researchers are now working to fabricate the nano-container structure and test whether they can achieve the predicted improvement experimentally.The team has already constructed a working proof-of-concept that measures magnetic fields by reading the spin states of the NV centers. The next challenge is achieving enough resolution to identify chemicals in extremely small fluid samples.From laboratory equipment to the battlefieldA fieldable version could eventually give personnel a portable way to assess unknown substances without transporting samples to a laboratory. APL says the goal would not necessarily be to replicate the precision of laboratory chemistry. Instead, the sensor could help answer practical questions in the field, such as whether an unknown substance presents a threat and what level of protective equipment may be required. The technology could potentially distinguish between chemically similar substances and identify biological threats, although the current work has not yet demonstrated those capabilities in a field-ready device.The researchers are also exploring applications beyond chemical and biological detection. NV-based quantum magnetometers could potentially be used for environmental monitoring, magnetic-field mapping for GPS-denied navigation, and low-frequency radio communications. APL researchers have also discussed possible applications aboard satellites and inside cryogenic systems.The current focus is on proving that nanoscale NMR can achieve the sensitivity needed for meaningful chemical detection. If the team succeeds, the result could transform a technology normally associated with large laboratory instruments into a compact quantum sensor that can be carried where the threat actually is.

title: US military orders 4,000 one-way attack UAVs with drone swarm control
content: Swarm Defense Technologies has received an order from the US Department of War for 4,000 Kiwi one-way attack drones, with a minimum value of $25 million including munitions. The Michigan-based company will build the aircraft for US military use.The order was placed under the Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, a challenge-based acquisition effort that uses military testing to evaluate small uncrewed aircraft before placing prototype delivery orders. The latest award follows the second Gauntlet competition at Fort Carson, Colorado.The Kiwi is a quadcopter configured for one-way attack missions. But the technology behind the order extends beyond the individual aircraft. Swarm Defense pairs its drones with software designed to let one operator control multiple aircraft simultaneously.The company will manufacture the drones at its 40,000-square-foot facility in Auburn Hills, Michigan. Swarm Defense grew out of Firefly Drone Shows, which has built more than 20,000 swarming drones since 2017 and shares engineering and manufacturing resources with the defense company.One operator controls swarmsThe company’s Strike Deck ground control software is designed to coordinate dozens of aircraft from a single operator. It automates waypoint navigation and relay-aircraft flight control while continuously managing flight paths to prevent aircraft from interfering with one another.The system also provides terminal guidance for the final approach to operator-designated targets. Target selection and engagement authorization, however, remain with human operators.“Combat units need to bring volume to the fight. Swarming allows a single pilot to accomplish what it normally takes several pilots to do,” said Adam Wright, President of Swarm Defense Technologies and a former Navy SEAL.Swarm Defense develops much of this technology in-house, including flight controllers, electronic speed controllers, power and battery-management electronics, embedded firmware, ground control software and swarm coordination technology.“Receiving an order for 4,000 Kiwi aircraft is a major milestone for Swarm Defense,” said Kyle Dorosz, CEO of Swarm Defense Technologies. “The Drone Dominance Program has placed its confidence in both our aircraft and our ability to deliver them at scale.”Kiwi extends beyond strike missionsAlthough the current order covers the one-way attack configuration, the Kiwi platform can be adapted for other missions. Swarm Defense says it can also perform intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, act as an airborne communications relay and serve as a reusable precision-dropper.The company is also working on a containerized drone deployment concept through a Phase I prototype agreement with the Defense Innovation Unit. The system would keep drones in a forward-deployed container until a remote operator launches them for ISR or strike missions.Swarm Defense’s broader software ecosystem includes Strike Deck, Swarm Studio mission-planning software and Swarm Threat Emulator systems used in Army, Air Force and Navy counter-drone training. Its current technology also focuses on coordinating large numbers of aircraft rather than treating each drone as an independent system.The 4,000-drone order therefore combines two parts of the company’s technology: high-volume drone manufacturing and software that allows a smaller number of operators to manage larger groups of aircraft.

title: US team to develop offshore system for uranium recovery from seawater
content: SuperCritical Materials has partnered with the University of Michigan to engineer and test offshore systems that could take its uranium-from-seawater technology toward industrial-scale deployment.The company already holds an exclusive license to a patented adsorbent technology designed to capture dissolved uranium from seawater. The new research will focus on the mechanical systems needed to deploy, expose and repeatedly retrieve that material in marine environments.The work will be led by Maha Haji, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Michigan and director of its Symbiotic Engineering and Analysis Laboratory. Her research includes designing offshore systems for recovering critical resources from the ocean.The partnership targets a major engineering challenge facing seawater uranium extraction. While the oceans contain an estimated 4.5 billion metric tons of dissolved uranium, a commercial system would need to handle large amounts of adsorbent efficiently through repeated offshore operating cycles.Taking extraction technology offshoreUniversity researchers will mechanically characterize SuperCritical’s uranium adsorbent and study how it responds to stresses during packing, deployment, ocean exposure and retrieval.They will also evaluate different ways to pack the material into nearshore systems before designing and building multiple prototypes of equipment capable of deploying and retrieving it.“The question is no longer simply whether uranium can be extracted from seawater. The question is whether the adsorbent can be deployed, exposed and retrieved efficiently and repeatedly at industrial scale,” said Alexander Canon Bryan, president and CEO of SuperCritical Materials.Testing is expected to take place at the University of Michigan’s Aaron Friedman Marine Hydrodynamics Laboratory. Its towing and wind-wave tanks can reproduce waves, currents and other marine conditions under controlled conditions.Researchers can therefore test multiple equipment designs and study their hydrodynamic behavior before moving to offshore trials.Haji has previously worked on this problem. During her doctoral research at MIT, she helped develop concepts for deploying and retrieving uranium adsorbents and participated in the fabrication and ocean testing of recovery systems.Building repeatable recovery systemsSuperCritical’s licensed technology uses adsorbent material that captures dissolved uranium as seawater passes across its surface. After a defined exposure period, the material is retrieved and processed to recover the captured uranium.The partnership does not change that underlying extraction process. Instead, it addresses how large quantities of the adsorbent could be physically handled and cycled through an offshore system reliably enough to support future commercial operations.“Extracting critical materials from the ocean requires more than a high-performing absorbent. It requires an offshore system that can operate efficiently, reliably and responsibly under demanding marine conditions,” Haji said.Results from the program are expected to guide SuperCritical’s future offshore pilot projects. The data will also feed into feasibility engineering, operating and capital cost modeling, and the design of future demonstration-scale systems.The company ultimately wants to determine whether seawater uranium recovery can operate competitively at industrial scale and contribute to US nuclear fuel supplies.

title: China sets first national testing standard for perovskite solar cells
content:
China sets first national testing standard for perovskite solar cells
China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) and Standardization Administration of China (SAC) have issued GB/T 6495.12-2026, the country's first national standard specifically for perovskite photovoltaics. Titled "Photovoltaic devices - Part 12: Measurement method for current-voltage (I-V) characteristics of perovskite photovoltaic cells and modules," the standard takes effect March 1, 2027, and applies to I-V measurements of terrestrial single-junction perovskite PV cells and modules, with potential use as a reference for multijunction perovskite devices as well.
The standard is designed to address capacitive effects and transient responses that can distort I-V measurements of perovskite devices in ways silicon cells don't exhibit. It sets out rapid I-V measurement procedures alongside additional quasi-steady-state verification methods for use where needed, including maximum power point tracking, ten-point quasi-steady-state fitting, and the asymptotic method, with ten-point quasi-steady-state fitting designated as the arbitration method in case of disputed results. It also specifies requirements for forward and reverse scans, spectral-mismatch correction, stabilization procedures, and efficiency calculations based on both total and aperture area.
The standard follows China's revised national energy efficiency standards for the broader PV supply chain, covering stages from polysilicon and monocrystalline silicon through PV modules and inverters, which take effect January 1, 2027. Together, the two sets of standards mark a step toward the kind of standardized, comparable measurement protocols that the perovskite industry has lacked as it moves from lab-scale efficiency records toward bankable, mass-manufactured products.

title: Swapping tin oxide for aluminum oxide enables perovskite tandem cells hit 26.9% efficiency
content:
Swapping tin oxide for aluminum oxide enables perovskite tandem cells hit 26.9% efficiency
Researchers at the University of Stuttgart, Forschungszentrum Jülich, INL - International Iberian Nanotechnology Laboratory, and
Solarlab Aiko Europe
have developed an ultrathin aluminum oxide (AlOₓ) buffer layer that protects perovskite solar cells from sputter damage during deposition of a transparent front electrode, while cutting material use and processing time compared with the industry-standard buffer layer.
In semi-transparent perovskite cells and perovskite-silicon tandem cells, a transparent conductive oxide front electrode is sputtered onto the device using a relatively aggressive process that damages the layers just beneath the surface. Buffer layers absorb that damage before it reaches the perovskite and its adjacent electron transport layer, most commonly a 10-20 nm-thick layer of tin oxide (SnOₓ) deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD) on top of the C₆₀ electron transport layer. But ALD growth of SnOₓ on C₆₀ tends to proceed in an island-like pattern rather than a smooth layer, leaving pinholes that require the buffer to be made thicker than would otherwise be needed. The team instead deposited a 3-5 nm-thick layer of aluminum oxide by ALD at a lower temperature of 75°C. Unlike the tin precursor used for SnOₓ, the trimethylaluminum precursor used to grow AlOₓ does not chemically attack the perovskite and instead passivates its surface, letting the layer grow more uniformly and with better coverage despite being far thinner.
Electron microscopy and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed that a 3 nm AlOₓ layer covers the underlying C₆₀/perovskite stack more completely than a 20 nm SnOₓ layer, and grazing-incidence X-ray diffraction showed the thin AlOₓ layer kept the perovskite's crystal structure undamaged through ITO sputtering - matching the protection offered by a SnOₓ layer seven times thicker.
Because aluminum oxide is a wide-bandgap insulator, a layer thick enough to block sputter damage would normally also block charge extraction. The team found their ALD-grown AlOₓ forms with a bandgap of 3.9 eV, well below the 6.9 eV reported for stoichiometric aluminum oxide, with defect-related electronic states within that gap that support charge transport via hopping. Devices with a 3 nm AlOₓ buffer showed higher conductivity (4.78 × 10⁻⁵ S/m) than those with a 20 nm SnOₓ buffer (1.21 × 10⁻⁵ S/m) and displayed ohmic rather than diode-like current-voltage behavior, indicating more efficient charge transfer despite AlOₓ's larger conduction-band offset with the C₆₀ layer.
Semi-transparent devices with the 3 nm AlOₓ buffer reached open-circuit voltages of 1.14 V and fill factors up to 82%, closely matching devices built with a 20 nm SnOₓ buffer (1.16 V, fill factor above 75%), and both buffer types exceeded 17% power conversion efficiency. A thinner 1.5 nm AlOₓ layer proved insufficient to prevent sputter damage, while layers thicker than 8 nm began to block charge extraction and reduce fill factor. Integrated into a two-terminal monolithic perovskite-silicon tandem cell, the 3 nm AlOₓ buffer delivered a stabilized efficiency of 26.9% with a 77% fill factor and negligible hysteresis, compared with a SnOₓ-buffered device that ranged between 26.6% and 27.2% depending on scan direction and showed a 3.76% hysteresis index.
The AlOₓ-buffered tandem cells also proved more robust under stress testing: unencapsulated devices retained 99% of their initial efficiency after 1,000 seconds at maximum power point, compared with 93% for SnOₓ-buffered devices; showed no efficiency loss after 70 minutes at 65°C, where SnOₓ-buffered cells lost 4%; and degraded only about 2% after 4 hours at 85°C, versus an 8% drop for SnOₓ-buffered devices. AlOₓ-buffered cells also resisted moisture-driven degradation better than their SnOₓ-buffered counterparts in a water-droplet test.
The authors noted that a 3 nm AlOₓ layer was thin enough to still allow efficient charge extraction across the C₆₀/ITO interface, despite aluminum oxide's insulating nature - a result they say was unexpected given how effectively the same thin layer blocked sputter damage. They conclude that while ALD is often seen as too slow a process for large-scale tandem manufacturing, the reduced material consumption and simpler deposition of an ultrathin AlOₓ buffer point toward a way to ease that bottleneck.

title: ACEN relinquishes Philippine solar projects over land, access issues - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Land acquisition and site-access problems have led Philippine renewables developer ACEN to abandon two early-stage solar projects with a combined potential capacity of about 456 MW.
Brian Publicover
23 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Rice terraces in the Philippines
ACEN Corp. said in a Sept. 18 disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange that its subsidiaries have given up solar energy operating contracts for projects in Quezon and Zambales provinces.
Abagat Energy Corp. relinquished its contract for a site in Pagbilao, Quezon, on Sept. 11 because of “significant land acquisition challenges affecting the project site.” SolarAce2 Energy Corp. relinquished its contract for Botolan, Zambales, on Sept. 17, citing site-access constraints.
The Philippine Department of Energy awarded the Pagbilao contract in August 2024 and the Botolan contract in June 2021. Its list of awarded solar projects, current to Dec. 31, 2025, puts their potential capacity at 336 MW and 120.30 MW, respectively, with both still in development.
ACEN said the cancellations have no material effect on its operations, as neither project had reached a final investment decision or begun commercial operations.
The department terminated 84 renewable energy contracts in 2025, representing about 5,372 MW of potential capacity, over failures to meet work-program requirements, auction terms, and other department standards. It said in December 2025 that a further 42 projects were under review and warned that noncompliant developers could face blacklisting and forfeiture of performance bonds.
ACEN reported about 7.5 GW of attributable renewable capacity, including capacity under construction, in its August investor presentation, and CEO John Eric Francia said in April the company was on track to exceed 8 GW by the end of 2026, according to Philippine daily
BusinessWorld
Land acquisition problems have delayed other Philippine solar projects. In October 2024, at least
53 of 105 renewable energy projects
under department review faced termination, and failure to secure possessory rights was among the reasons cited for delays. Earlier this month, the departments of energy and agriculture said they plan to separate
land suitable for solar development from areas reserved for food production
, under an agreement targeted for signing in October. The Philippines installed
899 MW of solar in 2025
, bringing cumulative capacity to 3,892 MW.
