BTU-Statiker liefert neue Erkenntnisse zu antikem Palast in Äthiopien

Wandkonstruktion am Computer nachgebaut: Die Grafik zeigt, wie die antiken Baumeister Holzbalken (magenta und blau; orange für die nächsthöhere Etage) in das Mauerwerk einbauten, um die Tragfähigkeit der Wände zu gewährleisten.
| Quelle:
Martin Drieschner, BTU
| Copyright:
Martin Drieschner, BTU
Download
Wie hoch könnten Gebäude vor rund 2.800 Jahren gewesen sein? Eine neue, interdisziplinäre Studie des DAI und der BTU liefert dazu erstmals belastbare statische Befunde. Im Juli 2026 erschien im Fachjournal Heritage (MDPI) die Publikation “Numerical Investigations of Timber-Reinforced Wall Constructions with Uncertain Material Parameters for the Ancient Palace Grat Be'al Gibri in Yeha, Ethiopia”.
Im Zentrum der Untersuchung von den Wissenschaftlern Vertr.-Prof. Dr.-Ing. Martin Drieschner, Fachgebiet Statik und Dynamik an der Brandenburgischen Technischen Universität Cottbus-Senftenberg (BTU), und Dipl.-Ing. Mike Schnelle, Außenstelle Sanaa des Deutschen Archäologischen Instituts (DAI), steht der Palast Grat Be'al Gibri in Yeha, im äthiopisch-eritreischen Hochland gelegen. Mit einer Grundfläche von etwa 60 mal 60 Metern gilt er als der größte bekannte Palastbau seiner Zeit in Südarabien und Ostafrika. Datiert auf etwa 800 v. Chr. wurde er bereits in der Antike durch einen Brand zerstört. Erhalten sind heute nur Teile des Erdgeschosses und des Podiums.
Holz-Mauerwerk-Verbund als Bauprinzip
Was den Bau geschichtlich besonders macht, ist sein Wandsystem: In das vermörtelte Bruchsteinmauerwerk wurden systematisch Holzbalken eingelegt und ausschließlich horizontal, abwechselnd in Längs- und Querrichtung der Wand verlegt. Diese und ähnliche Konstruktionsarten, “timber-laced masonry” genannt, sind im ersten Jahrtausend vor Christus in Südarabien und im nordöstlichen Afrika für mehrgeschossige Bauten weit verbreitet gewesen. Sie erinnern an moderne Hybridkonstruktionen unter Verwendung von Holz, wie sie heute etwa in Sydney, Hamburg oder Berlin beim nachhaltigen Hochhausbau eingesetzt werden oder in Planung sind.
3D-Modell unter Berücksichtigung von Materialunschärfe
Bislang beruhten Aussagen zur Höhe solcher Bauten vor allem auf historischen Quellen und bildlichen Darstellungen: Arabische Geschichtsschreiber berichten von Palästen mit bis zu 20 Stockwerken, südarabische Fels- und Wandmalereien zeigen turmartige, mehrgeschossige Gebäude. Eine ingenieurtechnische Überprüfung dieser Überlieferungen fehlte jedoch. Genau hier setzt die Kooperation zwischen dem DAI und der BTU an.
Für die Studie erstellten die Forschenden ein virtuelles 3D-Modell zweier exemplarischer Wandbereiche des Palastes – einer Wandecke und eines Türdurchgangs – und untersuchten deren Tragfähigkeit mithilfe der Finite-Elemente-Methode (FEM). Da viele Materialeigenschaften der antiken Baustoffe nicht exakt bekannt sind, kam ein Verfahren zur Berücksichtigung polymorpher Unschärfe in den Materialparametern zum Einsatz. Für die Berechnung wurde das selbstentwickelte Software-Tool PolyUQ verwendet.
Mindestens 19 Stockwerke statisch möglich
Das Ergebnis: Die Variation der Holzeigenschaften hat nur geringen Einfluss auf die Tragfähigkeit der Wände. Das untersuchte Wandsystem funktionierte robust. Nach ersten Berechnungen wäre eine Bebauung mit mindestens 19 Stockwerken statisch möglich gewesen. Damit hätte der Palast von Yeha durchaus Wolkenkratzer-Dimensionen erreicht. Aus den verbleibenden Tragreserven schließen die Autoren zudem, dass ein außergewöhnliches Ereignis – vermutlich der überlieferte Großbrand – für den Einsturz des Gebäudes verantwortlich gewesen sein muss.
Bauforschung trifft Ingenieurwissenschaft
„Das Projekt zeigt exemplarisch, welchen Erkenntnisgewinn interdisziplinäre Zusammenarbeit bringen kann", so Vertr.-Prof. Dr.-Ing. Martin Drieschner, Fachgebiet Statik und Dynamik an der BTU. „Für uns als Statiker ist besonders spannend, dass sich unsere Methoden aus dem modernen Ingenieurbau – etwa die Anwendung der FEM und die Modellierung unscharfer Materialparameter – eins zu eins auf eine 2.800 Jahre alte Konstruktion übertragen lassen. Das unterstreicht, wie leistungsfähig numerische Simulation auch jenseits klassischer Bauingenieur-Anwendungen ist."
Die Kooperation zwischen dem Fachgebiet Statik und Dynamik und der Außenstelle Sanaa des DAI ist Teil eines langfristig angelegten, von der Deutschen Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) geförderten äthiopisch-deutschen Forschungsprojekts zur Untersuchung des Fundplatzes Yeha im Norden Äthiopiens.
Publikation: Drieschner, M.; Schnelle, M. (2026): Numerical Investigations of Timber-Reinforced Wall Constructions with Uncertain Material Parameters for the Ancient Palace Grat Be'al Gibri in Yeha, Ethiopia. Heritage, 9(7), 270.

title: Hochbau und Bauen im Bestand: Millionenförderung vom Bund für Thüringer Forschungscluster

Hochbau und Bauen im Bestand: Millionenförderung vom Bund für Thüringer Forschungscluster

Am Freitag, 25. September 2026, überreichte Bundesbauministerin Verena Hubertz den drei Gründungsmitgliedern des Deutschen Forschungszentrums für zukunftsfähiges Bauen (DFZ Bau) in Berlin jeweils eine Millionen Euro Fördermittel.

Wie lassen sich bestehende Gebäude klimaneutraler, energieeffizienter und resilienter machen? Antworten erforscht das Thüringer Innovationszentrum für nachhaltiges Bauen. Gemeinsam mit der LEG Thüringen werden ab Oktober 2026 neue Bauweisen exemplarisch an Bestandsgebäuden in Erfurt und Gotha erprobt. Dafür erhält das Thüringer Konsortium, bestehend aus Bauhaus-Universität Weimar, Materialforschungs- und Prüfanstalt Weimar und IAB – Institut für Angewandte Bauforschung gemeinsam mit Industriepartnern, rund eine Millionen Euro Fördermittel vom Bund. Es ist das erste Projekt, welches im Rahmen des neu gegründeten Deutschen Forschungszentrums für zukunftsfähiges Bauen (DFZ Bau) umgesetzt wird.
Pro Jahr verursacht der Gebäudesektor in Deutschland rund 100 Millionen Tonnen Treibhausgasemissionen. Dabei ist ein Großteil der Gebäude bereits gebaut. Um Deutschlands Klimaziele bis 2045 zu erreichen, setzt das Bundesministerium für Wohnen, Stadtentwicklung und Bauwesen auf innovative Ansätze aus der Bauforschung. Am Freitag, 25. September 2026, überreichte Bundesbauministerin Verena Hubertz den drei Gründungsmitgliedern des Deutschen Forschungszentrums für zukunftsfähiges Bauen (DFZ Bau) – vertreten durch die Ministerpräsidenten Cem Özdemir und Mario Voigt sowie Dr. Andreas Handschuh, Chef der Sächsischen Staatskanzlei – in Berlin jeweils eine Millionen Euro Fördermittel für initiale Forschungsvorhaben in Sachsen, Baden-Württemberg und Thüringen.
»Bauen im Bestand ist eine zentrale Zukunftsaufgabe des Hochbaus. Gefragt sind Lösungen, die Gebäude nicht nur energieeffizienter machen, sondern sie zugleich an die Folgen des Klimawandels anpassen, Ressourcen schonen und ihre Lebensdauer verlängern. Innovative Bauforschung schafft dafür die Grundlagen: Sie untersucht neue Materialien und Konstruktionsweisen, entwickelt Technologien für die Sanierung und fragt danach, wie Gebäude langfristig klimaneutral, ressourcenschonend und resilient genutzt werden können«, erläutert Robert Fetter, Geschäftsführer des IAB Weimar. Gemeinsam mit Prof. Peter Benz, Präsident der Bauhaus-Universität Weimar vertritt er das Thüringer Innovationszentrum in Berlin. Auch Forschungsvorhaben von Prof. Viktor Mechtcherine (TU Dresden) und Prof. Achim Menges (Universität Stuttgart) werden vom Bund gefördert. Der Projektstart in Sachsen und Baden-Württemberg ist jeweils für Dezember 2026 anvisiert.
Bauwende beginnt in Thüringen
Mit der Gründung des Deutschen Forschungszentrums für zukunftsfähiges Bauen (DFZ Bau) an den drei Standorten Weimar (Thüringen), Dresden (Sachsen) und Stuttgart (Baden-Württemberg) werden dafür aktuell die nötigen Strukturen geschaffen. Bereits im April 2026 wurde der Grundstein für einen Technikumsneubau in Weimar gelegt, das Richtfest folgt im Dezember – diese Geschwindigkeit in der Umsetzung ist einer der Thüringer Erfolgsfaktoren.
Das Besondere: »In Weimar treffen jahrzehntelange Bauforschung, innovative Unternehmen und starke Partner aus Wissenschaft und Praxis aufeinander. Mit dem Deutschen Forschungszentrum für zukunftsfähiges Bauen wollen wir dieses Wissen schneller in konkrete Lösungen übersetzen – vom Labor auf die Baustelle und damit in die Praxis. So kann von Thüringen aus die Bauwende mitgestaltet werden«, erklärt Ministerpräsident Mario Voigt.
Praxistest in Erfurt und Gotha
An realen Bauobjekten sollen nun innovative Lösungen aus der Forschung getestet werden. Dabei handelt es sich um zwei Bauvorhaben der LEG in Erfurt und Gotha. Mithilfe digitaler Technologien soll zunächst der Zustand der Gebäude automatisiert erfasst werden. Aus den Daten wird ein digitales Modell erstellt, mit dessen Hilfe eine computergestützte Planung von Umbau- und Sanierungsprozessen in einem Building Information Model (BIM) ermöglicht wird. Zudem ist das Ziel, die beim Umbau anfallenden lokalen Baustoffe weitgehend vor Ort zu recyceln und Abbruchmaterial als Ersatzbaustoffe für den Wohnungsbau- und die energetische Sanierung einzusetzen sowie neue, klimaneutrale und nachwachsende Baustoffe zu verbauen.
Starker Forschungsverbund in Weimar
Das Thüringer Innovationszentrum für nachhaltiges Bauen (ThiZ-Bau) bündelt die Kompetenzen dreier etablierter Partner: des F.A. Finger-Institut für Baustoffkunde (FIB) an der Bauhaus-Universität Weimar, der Materialforschungs- und -prüfanstalt (MFPA) sowie des IAB Weimar. Gemeinsam decken sie die gesamte Innovationskette von der Grundlagenforschung bis zur anwendungsnahen Entwicklung ab. Mit rund 500 Forschenden verfügt Weimar bereits heute über eine außergewöhnlich hohe Kompetenzdichte im Bereich Bauforschung.
»Die Zukunft des Bauens entscheidet sich ganz wesentlich daran, wie wir mit dem umgehen, was bereits gebaut ist. Für die Bauhaus-Universität Weimar ist es deshalb besonders wichtig, Forschung nicht nur im Labor zu betreiben, sondern gemeinsam mit starken Partnern unter realen Bedingungen zu erproben. Das Thüringer Pilotprojekt zeigt exemplarisch, wofür der Forschungsstandort Weimar steht: Wir verbinden wissenschaftliche Exzellenz in den Bereichen Bauen, Materialien und Digitalisierung mit konkreten gesellschaftlichen Herausforderungen und bringen neue Erkenntnisse möglichst schnell in die Anwendung. Dass das erste Projekt des Deutschen Forschungszentrums für zukunftsfähiges Bauen aus diesem Verbund hervorgeht, unterstreicht die besondere Stärke und das Potenzial unseres Forschungsökosystems in Weimar.«, sagt der Weimarer Universitätspräsident Prof. Peter Benz.

Das Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT) hat den Hochleistungsrechner HoreKa 2 in Betrieb genommen. Das neue System unterstützt Forschende dabei, komplexe wissenschaftliche Fragestellungen etwa zu Klima, neuen Materialien, Teilchenphysik, Energie und Mobilität sowie KI-Forschung schneller zu bearbeiten. Dafür vereint es leistungsstarkes Hochleistungsrechnen und moderne KI-Technologien. Die Gesamtkosten der Anlage belaufen sich auf 17 Millionen Euro.
Den Supercomputer haben Vertreterinnen und Vertreter aus Wissenschaft, Politik und Wirtschaft am KIT-Campus Nord heute, Freitag, 25. September 2026, in einer Feierstunde gemeinsam in Betrieb genommen.
Neue Rechenpower für Forschung und Innovation
Moderne Forschung stellt Fragen, die sich ohne Hochleistungsrechnen nicht mehr beantworten lassen. Ob präzisere Klimamodelle, die Entwicklung neuer Werkstoffe, nachhaltige Technologien oder Anwendungen der nächsten Generation Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI): Für diese Aufgaben müssen große Datenmengen verarbeitet und hochkomplexe Simulationen durchgeführt werden. HoreKa 2 schafft die Voraussetzungen dafür.
Mit mehr als 42 000 Prozessorkernen, 300 KI-Beschleunigern und einer geplanten Spitzenleistung von rund 33 PetaFLOPS ermöglicht HoreKa 2 Berechnungen, die auf herkömmlichen Computersystemen Monate oder Jahre dauern würden. Das KIT stärkt damit seine Forschungsinfrastruktur, aber auch Forschende aus ganz Deutschland können das System nutzen.
„Wer bei Forschung und Innovation vorne bleiben will, braucht auch die beste Rechenleistung. Mit dem neuen Supercomputer HoreKA 2 am KIT bringen wir die nächste Generation des supereffizienten Hochleistungsrechnens an den Start. Das KIT ist als eines von neun bundesweiten Zentren des Nationalen Hochleistungsrechnens (NHR) ein wichtiger Partner und trägt mit seiner Kompetenz zur nationalen und europäischen digitalen Souveränität bei“, sagte Baden-Württembergs Wissenschaftsministerin Petra Olschowski.
„HoreKa 2 stärkt die digitale Leistungsfähigkeit des KIT und verbindet Spitzenforschung mit einem konsequenten Fokus auf Nachhaltigkeit. Damit schaffen wir die Voraussetzungen, um datenintensive Forschung und moderne KI-Anwendungen energieeffizient und nachhaltig zu betreiben“, sagt Professorin Kora Kristof, Vizepräsidentin Digitalisierung und Nachhaltigkeit des KIT.
Hochleistungsrechner für Forschung aller Fachrichtungen
„Von dem neuen System profitieren Forschende aus nahezu allen Fachgebieten“, sagt Professor Martin Frank, Mitglied des Direktoriums des Scientific Computing Center (SCC) des KIT. „Mit dem neuen System verdoppeln wir die Rechenleistung für Simulationen und KI-Anwendungen.“
Neben den Schwerpunkten Erdsystemwissenschaften, Ingenieurwesen, Materialwissenschaften und Teilchenphysik stehen die Rechenkapazitäten auch zahlreichen weiteren Disziplinen zur Verfügung. Die integrierten Grafikprozessoren sind speziell für KI-Anwendungen ausgelegt, die inzwischen in fast allen Bereichen der Wissenschaft zum Einsatz kommen.
Nachhaltiges Hochleistungsrechnen
Bei der Entwicklung und Beschaffung standen Leistungsfähigkeit und Energieeffizienz gleichermaßen im Fokus. HoreKa 2 zählt zu den energieeffizientesten Hochleistungsrechnern seiner Leistungsklasse weltweit. Zur Kühlung nutzt das System Heißwasser, wodurch eine besonders energieeffiziente Betriebsweise und eine ganzjährige freie Rückkühlung möglich sind. Die Stromversorgung am Campus Nord des KIT erfolgt zu 100 Prozent aus erneuerbaren Energien. Zusätzlich leisten die Kraft-Wärme-Kopplungs- und Photovoltaikanlagen einen Beitrag zur nachhaltigen Energieversorgung.
Ausführliche Bildunterschrift:
Gemeinsame Einweihung des neuen Hochleistungsrechners HoreKa 2
(Zu sehen sind (v.l.n.r.): Pascal Friederich, Professor am KIT, Oliver Rootsey, General Manager von Lenovo für Deutschland und Österreich, Kora Kristof, Vizepräsidentin Digitalisierung und Nachhaltigkeit des KIT, Petra Olschowski, Wissenschaftsministerin von Baden-Württemberg und Martin Frank, Direktor des Scientific Computing Center des KIT. (Foto: Cynthia Ruf, KIT)
Im Dialog mit der Gesellschaft entwickelt das KIT Lösungen für große Herausforderungen – von Klimawandel, Energiewende und nachhaltigem Umgang mit natürlichen Ressourcen bis hin zu Künstlicher Intelligenz, technologischer Souveränität und demografischem Wandel. Als Die Universität in der Helmholtz-Gemeinschaft vereint das KIT wissenschaftliche Exzellenz vom Erkenntnisgewinn bis zur Anwendungsorientierung unter einem Dach – und ist damit in einer einzigartigen Position, diese Transformation voranzutreiben. Damit bietet das KIT als Exzellenzuniversität seinen mehr als 10 000 Mitarbeitenden sowie seinen 23 000 Studierenden herausragende Möglichkeiten, eine nachhaltige und resiliente Zukunft zu gestalten. Vom Schrott zum Schatz: KI bewertet ausgediente Komponenten - Auftakt des EU-Projekts „RESURRECTION“

Mehr als 30 Fachleute aus ganz Europa kamen zum Kick-off des Forschungsprojekts RESURRECTION an der Hochschule Kempten zusammen
| Quelle:
David Sieblitz
| Copyright:
Hochschule Kempten/David Sieblitz
Download
Reparieren, wiederverwenden, aufbereiten oder recyceln: Was soll mit ausgedienten technischen Produkten und ihren Komponenten geschehen, etwa mit Hochvoltbatterien aus Fahrzeugen, Waschmaschinen oder Industrierobotern? Belastbare Antworten auf diese Frage sucht das europäische Forschungsprojekt „RESURRECTION“. Die Hochschule Kempten entwickelt dafür KI-Verfahren, die den Zustand gebrauchter Komponenten bewerten und vorhersagen, wie lange sie noch genutzt werden können.
Den Kemptener Projektbeitrag leitet Prof. Dr.-Ing. Peter Wurster am EPT – Institut für Effiziente Produktionstechnik. Die Koordination des Verbunds mit 16 Partnern aus elf Nationen liegt bei der Technischen Universität Dortmund. Zum Projektauftakt trafen sich am 22. und 23. September mehr als 30 Fachleute aus ganz Europa in Kempten. Die Europäische Union fördert RESURRECTION im Rahmen des Forschungs- und Innovationsprogramms Horizon Europe für vier Jahre mit knapp sieben Millionen Euro. Auf die Hochschule Kempten entfallen davon rund 581.000 Euro.
Kreislaufwirtschaft braucht verlässliche Entscheidungen
Auch wenn ein Gerät oder eine Maschine ausgedient hat, stecken darin oft noch wertvolle Komponenten. Eine Schlüsselrolle für die Kreislaufwirtschaft spielt deshalb das sogenannte Remanufacturing, also die industrielle Wiederaufarbeitung, bei der gebrauchte Produkte zerlegt, geprüft, instandgesetzt und wieder auf den Stand eines Neuprodukts gebracht werden. Ob sich eine Komponente dafür eignet, beurteilen Fachkräfte bislang meist von Hand. Bei so unterschiedlich beanspruchten Altteilen ist das zeitaufwendig, und die Ergebnisse fallen nicht immer einheitlich aus.
Hier setzt RESURRECTION an: Das Projekt verbindet Robotik, künstliche Intelligenz und digitale Infrastrukturen, um gebrauchte Produkte zu untersuchen, robotergestützt zu zerlegen und fundierte Entscheidungen über ihre weitere Verwendung zu ermöglichen. Eine zentrale Grundlage dafür sind Digitale Produktpässe, die wesentliche Informationen bündeln, und Digitale Zwillinge, die Geräte und Prozesse virtuell abbilden. Damit bleibt über den gesamten Lebenszyklus erkennbar, woher eine Komponente stammt und welche Stationen sie bereits durchlaufen hat.
Ergänzend entstehen Trainingsangebote, die Beschäftigte auf die Zusammenarbeit mit KI- und Robotiksystemen vorbereiten. Erprobt werden die Lösungen in vier Anwendungsbereichen: Hochvoltbatterien aus Elektrofahrzeugen, Waschmaschinen, Industrieroboter und Telekommunikationsgeräte wie Modems. Ziel ist es, Remanufacturing effizienter und in größerem Maßstab umzusetzen, den Wert von Materialien und Komponenten länger zu erhalten und Elektroschrott zu reduzieren.
KI bewertet Zustand und Restnutzungsdauer
Die Hochschule Kempten übernimmt im Projekt die Federführung bei der sogenannten Datenfusion. Dabei werden Kamerabilder und weitere Sensordaten zusammengeführt und ausgewertet. Auf dieser Grundlage entwickelt das EPT-Team KI-basierte Modelle, die den Zustand einer Komponente bewerten und ihre verbleibende Nutzungsdauer vorhersagen. Bei gebrauchten Industrierobotern etwa gilt es abzuschätzen, wie lange Lager und Getriebe noch halten. Die Verfahren sind dabei nicht auf Roboter beschränkt, sondern für alle vier Anwendungsbereiche von Bedeutung, von der Hochvoltbatterie bis hin zum Modem. Zudem erarbeitet das Team Referenzdatensätze sowie Werkzeuge, die die Ergebnisse der KI für Anwenderinnen und Anwender nachvollziehbar machen. Damit liefert das EPT einen inhaltlichen Kern des Gesamtprojekts. Darauf aufbauend entsteht im Verbund ein Entscheidungssystem, das Empfehlungen für den weiteren Weg einer Komponente gibt.
„Die zentrale Herausforderung besteht darin, sehr unterschiedliche Daten aus verschiedenen Sensoren und Produkten entlang der gesamten Wertschöpfungskette zusammenzuführen“, erläutert Projektleiter Prof. Wurster. Gelingt das, können Unternehmen künftig zuverlässig und nachvollziehbar entscheiden, ob sich eine Komponente für die Reparatur, Wiederverwendung, Aufbereitung oder das Recycling eignet.
Erstes Treffen in Kempten
Beim Kick-off lernten sich die beteiligten Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler sowie Fachleute aus der Industrie erstmals persönlich kennen. „Die Kreislaufwirtschaft kann eine wichtige Antwort auf viele der drängendsten Herausforderungen unserer Zeit sein“, betonte Prof. Wurster zur Begrüßung. Entschei-dend sei, technische Lösungen mit den Menschen zu verbinden, die mit ihnen arbeiten.
Das Koordinationsteam der TU Dortmund präsentierte anschließend die Ziele und den Aufbau von RESURRECTION. In kurzen Vorstellungsrunden erläuterten die beteiligten Partner ihre Aufgaben im Projekt und ihre Erwartungen an die Zusammenarbeit.
Das Projekt mit dem vollständigen Titel „Robotics and AI-assisted Decision Support for Efficient and Sustainable Remanufacturing and Refurbishment in Electronics towards Circular Transformation“ läuft bis Ende August 2030.
Über das EPT – Institut für Effiziente Produktionstechnik
Das EPT der Hochschule Kempten ist eine anwendungsorientierte, interdisziplinäre Forschungseinrichtung an der Schnittstelle zwischen Wissenschaft und Industrie. Das Institut arbeitet gemeinsam mit Industriepartnern, anderen For-schungseinrichtungen und Verbänden an einer nachhaltigen Verbesserung von Fertigungsverfahren, einer Optimierung der Produktionstechnologien sowie an der Anpassung der jeweiligen Produkte an markt- und gesellschaftspolitische Anforderungen. www.hs-kempten.de/ept.
Über Horizon Europe
Horizon Europe ist das Rahmenprogramm der Europäischen Union für Forschung und Innovation. RESURRECTION wird im Themenbereich „Integrated approaches for remanufacturing“ der europäischen Partnerschaft „Made in Europe“ gefördert.
Das Projekt RESURRECTION (Finanzhilfevereinbarung Nr. 101294921) wird im Rahmen des Programms Horizon Europe (ko-)finanziert. Die geäußerten Ansichten und Meinungen sind jedoch ausschließlich die der Autorinnen und Autoren und spiegeln nicht notwendigerweise die Ansichten der Europäischen Union oder der European Health and Digital Executive Agency wider. Weder die Europäische Union noch die Bewilligungsbehörde können dafür verantwortlich gemacht

title: Wie Plattformen die Stadt verändern
content:
Wie Plattformen die Stadt verändern
Weizenbaum-Institut lädt zur Keynote „The City and the Platform“ am 30. September an der TU Berlin ein
Was passiert mit Städten, wenn digitale Plattformen zunehmend bestimmen, wie Menschen Orte wahrnehmen, nutzen und sich über ihr Umfeld austauschen? Mit dieser Frage beschäftigt sich die Keynote „The City and the Platform“ am 30. September 2026 an der TU Berlin. Der Stadtgeograf Professor Justus Uitermark von der Universität Amsterdam und die Kommunikationswissenschaftlerin Dr. Daniela Stoltenberg vom Weizenbaum-Institut diskutieren, wie digitale Plattformen städtisches Leben verändern – und wie Städte und ihre Bewohner*innen darauf reagieren.
Justus Uitermark stellt in seinem Beitrag „Will Cities Survive Platforms?“ das Konzept des „Plattform-Urbanismus“ infrage. Städte und digitale Plattformen seien grundverschiedene komplexe Systeme, die strukturell in Spannung zueinander stehen. Anhand von TikTok, Google Maps und Instagram zeigt Uitermark, wie Plattformlogiken urbane Orte und Netzwerke verändern und unter Druck setzen. Zugleich geht er der Frage nach, wie Städte und ihre Bewohner*innen damit umgehen – etwa durch kollektiven Widerstand oder alltägliche Praktiken, mit denen sie sich den Vorgaben der Plattformen entziehen.
Daniela Stoltenberg forscht an der DFG-geförderten Nachwuchsgruppe „Local Digital Public Spheres“ des Weizenbaum-Instituts zu lokaler politischer Kommunikation in sozialen Medien. Sie untersucht unter anderem Wohnraum-Diskurse, Formen des digitalen Aktivismus und Auseinandersetzungen um politisch umkämpfte Orte. Im Zentrum steht das Konzept der „Platform Affordances“: die Frage, wie technische Möglichkeiten digitaler Plattformen und die Praktiken ihrer Nutzer*innen zusammenwirken und die Bedeutung digitaler Medien für das lokale Zusammenleben beeinflussen.

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved lie detector, according to a Department of Defense budget request.
The program, called “Polygraph+” or “Polygraph Next,” will focus on scoring algorithms that use AI and machine learning, as well as a technique called “standoff sensing,” which can take physiological readings from a person without attaching a device to them.
The project aims to improve the accuracy and reliability of polygraph assessments. But it could just be the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies.
—Amit Katwala
Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients
Around this time last year, a hot mic caught Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping discussing the possibility of living forever. “With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Putin reportedly said.
He seemed to be referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, supported by experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones. Unfortunately for Putin, new research on transplanted hearts pours a little cold water on this idea. But it also offers useful insights for organ transplantation.
Find out what the research reveals about the limits of rejuvenation.
—Jessica Hamzelou

The US has spent billions building a “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along its southern border, promising to detect and apprehend border crossers and save lives. title: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector
content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The US government wants to spend $30.3 million over the next five years on an improved form of lie detector, according to a
Department of Defense budget request
. The program, called Polygraph+ or Polygraph Next, will focus on scoring algorithms that use artificial intelligence and machine learning and on a technique called “standoff sensing,” which refers to the ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to a subject’s person.
According to details of the budget document, which were first reported by
Inside Defense
, the project will “modernize federal polygraph and credibility assessment technologies” to improve their accuracy and reliability. But the project may be just the latest in a long line of failed attempts to use technology to detect lies. “It’s a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” says Kyri Kotsoglou, a legal scholar at Northumbria University in the UK who studies the use of polygraphs in the justice system.
The move comes at a time of high tension within the department. Under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon has been increasingly turning to polygraph tests in an attempt to find the sources of alleged leaks to the press. In September, the
New York Times
reported that
around 50 officers
on the Joint Staff had been given polygraph tests after news coverage reported on the depletion of US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.
Polygraph+ will be run by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), which conducts background checks for the federal government. According to the budget document, which has not yet been approved by Congress, the new technology will be used for vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” It is not yet clear which specific technologies will be used, and the DCSA did not respond to a request for more information.
But other Pentagon efforts offer potential clues. In 2023, the department’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) ran an open submission process to find companies with products that could be used for deception detection.
It selected
two companies to build prototypes
: Presage Technologies, which claims to be able to measure heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras, and Altec Research, a medical sensor company now branching out into non-contact sensing technologies. A
screenshot
of Altec’s prototype technology released by the DIU shows that it tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity. Presage Technologies and Altec Research did not respond to requests for comment. The DIU declined to comment.
Altec Research has built a prototype that tracks head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity.
ALTEC RESEARCH
Current lie detection technology has barely changed since the polygraph was
invented in the 1920s
. Examiners rely on blood pressure, pulse, breathing, and sweat measurements to determine if someone is lying. They make judgments about the veracity of respondents’ replies on the basis of differences in their physiological response to baseline questions like “Is the sky blue?” and target questions like “Have you ever committed a crime?”
The federal government conducts tens of thousands of the tests each year while screening employees, but the reliability of this technology has been repeatedly challenged—and its results are rarely admissible in court. In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment
concluded
that there was very limited evidence supporting the polygraph’s use for screening employees, and in
, the US National Research Council (NRC) said evidence for its efficacy was “weak at best.”
Research
suggests humans can spot a lie just over half the time without any technical assistance. The American Polygraph Association
the polygraph is between 80% and 94% accurate. But the 2003 NRC report pointed out that a screening test with this level of accuracy could still lead to a lot of mistakes. The DOD employs 2.8 million people; an imperfect system applied at that scale could end up falsely accusing tens of thousands.
There are other issues too. Polygraph interpretations are often subjective:
Different examiners get wildly different results
, and people from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive. What’s more, with training it’s possible for interviewees to learn a variety of countermeasures that can help beat the test; for example, they may artificially heighten their physiological response to baseline questions by stepping on a pin hidden in their shoe.
“If you know how it works, you can beat it,” says Sophie van der Zee, an associate professor who studies deception at Erasmus University in Rotterdam. She says the machine’s biggest effect is deterrence—often, subjects confess before it even begins. “But that only works if people think a polygraph works,” she points out.
Various new strategies for lie detection have been attempted
over the decades
, with technologies ranging from thermal cameras to pupil trackers to brain scans. None of them have yielded reliable results outside the lab. The problem is that there’s no single telltale sign of lying that’s true for everyone all the time. “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose,” says van der Zee.
AI could theoretically
improve polygraphs
if it could find patterns in the data that examiners can’t. AI algorithms are also more likely to be used for “multi-modal” deception detection, which seeks to combine multiple measurements into an overall deception “score” that is harder for people to game. Three things are happening under the surface that lie detection tries to home in on, van der Zee says: physiological stress, cognitive load, and the conscious efforts people make to conceal the fact that they’re lying. Current polygraph technology tackles only one.
“The more you can have combined methods that approach it from these three different angles, the more successful you will be,” van der Zee says. This isn’t a new concept—in the 2000s, researchers at Manchester Metropolitan University in the UK developed a system called
Silent Talker
that generated a deception score from video footage. This was later folded into iBorderCtrl, an EU-funded pilot program. In the US, a project called AVATAR incorporated eye tracking, voice analysis, and body movement detection into a tool for use at border crossings. All these projects have quietly faded away.
Kotsoglou says combining AI and the polygraph is “the worst of both worlds” because it adds uncertainty on top of invalidity. Even if AI or machine learning can spot previously unseen patterns in physiological data, it won’t be able to reliably link them to lying because there is no real ground truth.
“Even if you have all the records in the world from polygraph tests, you don't know whether those polygraph tests are right or not,” says Marion Oswald, a professor of law who has written with Kotsoglou on the use of polygraphs in the justice system. She fears that new forms of lie detection will, like the polygraph, be used more as a psychological prop than a scientific tool.
“It seems very much a response to the concern of the current administration to leaks and perceived lack of loyalty,” says Oswald. “[Lie detection is] being used as a threat, to intimidate and force people to confess to things, as opposed to anything that's actually getting valid information.”

title: Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients
content:
Young organs may not be a fountain of youth for recipients
New studies pour cold water on a prominent rejuvenation idea.
Around this time last year I was attending an aging conference in Manchester, listening to a talk about fly aging, when my phone started pinging. News outlets were reporting that a hot mic had caught Russia’s and China’s leaders discussing the possibility of living forever.
“With the developments of biotechnology, human organs can be continuously transplanted, and people can live younger and younger, and even achieve immortality,” Russia’s Vladimir Putin reportedly told China’s Xi Jinping.
He seems to have been referring to the “replacement” theory of longevity, which has been supported by multiple experiments that involved physically stitching young mice to old ones. Something about the young blood rejuvenated the old mice. Perhaps young organs could rejuvenate world leaders in their 70s, too.
Unfortunately for Putin, new research pours a little cold water on this idea. Studies on transplanted hearts in both mice and humans suggest that new hearts soon adopt the biological age of the recipient, no matter how young they were to begin with. The finding could be important for transplantation, but it also highlights just how complex aging—and rejuvenation—are.
Jesse Poganik at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston is one of the many scientists trying to understand exactly what it is about the bodies of young mice that rejuvenates old ones. Plenty of research has focused on seeking the secrets of youth in young blood. But what if it’s something about young organs instead?
To find out, he and his colleagues performed a set of heart transplants in mice. In humans, heart transplants typically involve removing a damaged or injured heart and replacing it with another from a donor who is usually much younger than the recipient. (When Poganik assessed hospital records, he found that most recipients were about 20 years older than their donors.)
The mouse transplants were different: Mice received a second heart, implanted in the neck—a procedure that’s slightly simpler and allows scientists to compare the new hearts with the existing ones. In some cases, young adult mice were given a heart from a middle-aged donor. In others, middle-aged mice got young hearts.
The team used a trio of “aging clocks”—molecular tools used to estimate the biological ages of tissues and whole organisms—to assess whether the additional hearts affected the mice in any way. These clocks were good at predicting the chronological age of mice that didn’t get new hearts.
Poganik says he was expecting to see a reciprocal effect, and that young hearts might benefit older animals, for example. In previous work by other members of his team, young mice that got old hearts experienced a buildup of senescent cells in their other organs. These cells are thought to contribute to the aging process, suggesting that receiving an old organ might prematurely age an animal.
But that’s not what he found. When he and his colleagues analyzed the transplanted hearts between four and six months after surgery, they found that the hearts seemed to have adopted the biological age of the recipients. Young hearts got older, and old hearts got younger. “The environment of the transplanted organ really dictates how it seems to behave biologically,” he says. The findings were published online at bioRxiv last week.
The team also looked at each mouse’s blood and other organs—including its original heart—and were surprised to find that they seemed to be unaffected by the presence of the new heart, despite the age of its donor.
The finding was backed up by data from human heart transplants. People who receive a donor heart must typically undergo a series of heart biopsies after surgery. The tiny pieces of heart tissue collected from people who had heart transplants at Brigham and Women’s have been stored for decades. And when Poganik and his colleagues tested their biological ages with the aging clocks, they found a similar pattern: No matter the age of the donor, a new heart quickly adopts the biological age of the person who received it.
It’s not clear why this is, but João Pedro de Magalhães, who studies aging at the University of Birmingham in the UK and was not involved in the study, thinks it might have something to do with the recipient’s immune system. Perhaps immune cells circulating in the blood might affect markers of aging in the new organ, he says.
Perhaps the potential rejuvenating effects of a young heart end up being diluted by all the other aged components of an older body, Poganik suggests. Or maybe a single organ just isn’t enough to see an effect.
Poganik hopes his finding will encourage surgeons to consider using hearts from older donors, many of which are discarded on the assumption they won’t function as well. (Machines used to preserve organs before transplantation are changing that already—and Poganik has worked on another study showing that these devices seem to rejuvenate donor livers to some extent.)
But the study also highlights just how complicated aging is. If organs seem to be getting older by one measure but not by another, how can we get a full picture of the biological age of an organ, or a person?
This complexity means that scientists are not likely to discover a true way to completely reverse aging, says Poganik. “That would mean that every aspect of aging has to go back in time,” he says. Reversing DNA damage, structural damage, and all the other degradations that are part of the aging package, across all our various cells and tissues, presents an enormous challenge.
“There are aspects of biological age that are probably reversible, and there are aspects that are probably not,” he says. Sorry, Putin.

title: Amazon & WEF: Innovation in Fashion Supply Chains
content:
Amazon & WEF: Innovation in Fashion Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
A cross-industry initiative has been launched to innovate fashion supply chains
In a cross-industry initiative, the Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has been launched, bringing together Amazon, Stella McCartney and World Economic Forum
Fashion supply chains are vast, interconnected networks which include raw material sourcing, design and final sale. Along the way, manufacturing and distribution are involved, adding further complexities to the chain.
The fashion industry faces significant challenges, including
major traceability gaps
beyond Tier-1, resulting in labour malpractices and poor environmental solutions.
In order to make the industry more responsible, The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has been founded.
Supply chain collaboration
At present,
the fashion industry
accounts for 2-8% of global greenhouse gas emissions, as well as contributing to significant plastic use, clothing waste, pollution, water consumption and microplastics. Within leading fashion brands, more than 95% of GHG emissions are Scope 3, caused by fragmented supply chains with poor transparency.
As climate events become more widespread, organisations need to act in order to reduce their impact and develop sustainable solutions for a more resilient future.
In a cross-industry collaboration, The Climate Pledge, Amazon, Stella McCartney and Canopy have co-founded The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition. The coalition has support from the World Economic Forum and supports more than 60 Climate Pledge signatories.
It is a mass collaborative coalition, including fashion brands, manufacturers, retailers and innovators.
The aim is to support each other and reach net-zero carbon by 2040. By integrating new financing models and tools such as the Fashion Coalition Lever Library, the coalition aims to scale the use of sustainable materials and manufacturing processes across the industry. In doing so, the fashion supply chain environmental impact should be significantly reduced.
"Transitions of this scale don't happen brand by brand, they happen when an industry moves together,” explains Nicole Rycroft, Founder and Executive Director of Canopy.
“By diversifying fashion's fibre basket with emerging Next Gen materials, this coalition builds more resilient supply chains, reduces sourcing risk and keeps vital forests standing.”
Nicole Rycroft, Founder and Executive Director of Canopy
Industry figures
The fashion industry produces 2-8% of global greenhouse gas emissions annually
Scope 3 emissions account for 95% of leading fashion brands' total carbon footprint
More than 60 Climate Pledge signatories receive support through the coalition
30+ brands and suppliers collaborated to build The Fashion Coalition Lever Library
92 million tonnes of textile waste is generated worldwide each year (UNEP, 2024)
Fashion supply chains operate across 60+ industries through coalition partnerships
Sustainability innovation
At present, the materials and processes that could make a positive impact are too fragmented, costly or too scarce to be able to be implemented at scale. The coalition, therefore, is working to target early innovation, making it a standard process in the industry.
“Making sustainable materials the default rather than the premium choice requires entire value chains to move together,” says Clemence Schmid, Head of Circular Economy Transformation & Director, Global Plastic Action Partnership at World Economic Forum.
“The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition is designed to enable that alignment to ultimately increase the confidence that can unlock investment to scale. This is how we can accelerate adoption today, not a decade from now.”
Clemence Schmid, Head of Circular Economy Transformation & Director, Global Plastic Action Partnership at World Economic Forum
The coalition will be supporting development, commercialisation and adoption of more sustainable materials and processes. This includes using waste feedstocks in materials, as well as driving processes that reduce water use and emissions.
Through changing industry standards, the coalition aims to transform the industry.
"For over two decades, I've worked alongside innovators proving that fashion can be made differently. The solutions already exist. What's been missing is the industry-wide commitment to help them scale,” explains Stella McCartney, Founder and Creative Director at Stella McCartney.
“The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition is about turning innovation into infrastructure, creating real demand for the next generation of materials and giving the pioneers a pathway from
breakthrough to industry standard
Stella McCartney, founder Stella McCartney
Cross-industry impact
The Climate Pledge was co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019 and has since grown to include more than 700 signatories across more than 60+ industries. Much of these industries have some relation with the fashion supply chain, creating a complex cross-sector network.
The coalition builds on a
model of collaboration
, with an industry that relies so heavily on a wealth of resources. Organisations across every part of the fashion supply chain are brought into this network, working towards the development of practical tools and lower-carbon supply chains, through innovative materials and technologies.
"Fashion has no shortage of ambition on sustainability,” states Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon.
Kara Hurst, Chief Sustainability Officer at Amazon
“People are already looking for more sustainable options when they shop, and now the industry needs to deliver at scale. Through The Climate Pledge, we're bringing together more than 60
fashion and retail brands
, manufacturers, and innovators to help make that happen."
WEF is helping the coalition to develop blended financing mechanisms which will help unlock large-scale investments. As a result, it will be easier to make sustainable materials competitive and grow them to scale.
More than 30 brands and suppliers consulted on the development of the Fashion Coalition Lever Library – a network to help companies identify the solutions, innovators and materials which will have a strong impact on their supply chain.
The coalition demonstrates how networks can come together to make a difference, offering real-world evidence for environmental transformation.
Through this, the fashion industry is working in tandem to remove waste from its supply chain and minimise its negative impact on the environment.
This is how we can accelerate adoption today, not a decade from now.
Clemence Schmid, Head of Circular Economy Transformation & Director, Global Plastic Action Partnership at World Economic Forum
Key companies
CEO: Andy Jassy
HQ: Washington, US
Amazon is a multinational technology company founded by Jeff Bezos in 1994, initially as an online bookstore. It has evolved into the world's largest e-commerce platform, offering cloud computing services (AWS), streaming entertainment, and artificial intelligence solutions. Amazon also operates physical retail stores and has made significant investments in sustainable initiatives, including co-founding The Climate Pledge to achieve net-zero carbon emissions.
Stella McCartney
CEO: Tom Mendenhall
HQ: London, UK
Stella McCartney is a British luxury fashion house founded in 2001 by designer Stella McCartney. The brand is renowned for pioneering sustainable and ethical practices in high fashion, never using leather, fur, feathers, or skin. McCartney emphasizes innovative materials, circular design, and transparency. The company partners with environmental organizations and uses regenerative agriculture practices, setting industry standards for responsible luxury fashion.
The Climate Pledge
The Climate Pledge is a commitment co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019, pledging to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2040—ten years ahead of the Paris Agreement. Signatories commit to regular reporting, carbon elimination strategies, and credible offset measures. The initiative encourages cross-industry collaboration, with hundreds of companies participating. It represents a business-led approach to combating climate change through measurable, accountable action.
World Economic Forum
CEO: Alois Zwinggi
HQ: Cologny, Switzerland
The World Economic Forum is an international organization founded in 1971, headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. It brings together political, business, cultural, and societal leaders to shape global, regional, and industry agendas. Best known for its annual meeting in Davos, the WEF addresses critical issues including economic development, climate change, healthcare, and technology. It facilitates public-private cooperation and promotes stakeholder capitalism.
Founder and Executive Director: Nicole Rycroft
HQ: Vancouver, Canada
Canopy is a Canadian environmental nonprofit organization founded in 1999, dedicated to protecting ancient and endangered forests. The organization collaborates with over 750 companies to develop forest-friendly supply chains, particularly in fashion, packaging, and publishing industries. Canopy's CanopyStyle initiative works with brands to eliminate ancient forest fiber from fabrics. Their innovative solutions include supporting Next Generation alternatives like agricultural residue-based materials.
Anna Sui
CEO: Anna Sui
HQ: New York, US
Anna Sui is an American fashion designer and brand founded in 1980, known for bohemian-inspired designs blending vintage Americana, rock-and-roll aesthetics, and global influences. Sui's distinctive style features bold prints, rich colors, and eclectic patterns. The brand has expanded to include cosmetics, accessories, and fragrances. Sui has received numerous accolades, including the CFDA Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award, solidifying her iconic status.
Bananatex
CEO: Hannes Schoenegge
HQ: Zug, Switzerland
Bananatex is the world's first technical fabric made entirely from banana plants, developed by Swiss bag brand QWSTION in collaboration with yarn specialist Lean Plastics Technologies. The durable, waterproof material is cultivated in the Philippines using natural ecosystem forestry, requiring no pesticides or additional water. Bananatex is biodegradable and compostable, offering a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based technical fabrics for bags, accessories, and outdoor gear.
Vestiaire Collective
CEO: Bernard Osta
HQ: Paris, France
Vestiaire Collective is a global online marketplace for pre-owned luxury fashion founded in 2009 in Paris. The platform enables buying and selling authenticated designer items, promoting circular fashion and extending garment lifecycles. With millions of members worldwide, Vestiaire authenticates products, ensuring quality and legitimacy. The company has achieved B Corporation certification, demonstrating commitment to sustainability by reducing fashion waste and encouraging conscious luxury consumption.

Holly Sullivan, VP of Economic Development at Amazon, says a $100m Greenwood facility strengthens its robotics supply chain while creating 300 skilled jobs
Amazon has announced plans to invest more than US$100m in a new 585,000 square-foot
advanced manufacturing
facility in Greenwood, Indiana.
The investment will create 300
skilled manufacturing
and engineering jobs, with average salaries of nearly US$100,000 annually.
According to Amazon, it supports more than 27,000 direct jobs and 40,000 indirect jobs across the state, contributing more than US$35bn to Indiana's GDP.
“We're thrilled to bring 300 advanced manufacturing jobs to Greenwood, Indiana, and to continue investing in growth and opportunities across the state,” says Holly Sullivan, Vice President of Economic Development at Amazon. “This facility represents a significant investment in the Indianapolis community that will create jobs with a median salary well above the regional average.”
Amazon's Greenwood Investment
Amazon is investing more than US$100m in a new manufacturing facility in Greenwood, Indiana
The facility will create 300 skilled manufacturing and engineering jobs
Workers will earn an average salary of nearly US$100,000 per year
The 585,000-square-foot site is expected to launch by 2028
Amazon has invested more than US$40bn in Indiana since 2008
Holly Sullivan, VP of Economic Development at Amazon. Credit: Jacky Akbari via LinkedIn
Inside Amazon's Greenwood manufacturing plant
The facility will integrate advanced fabrication, robotic welding, automated powder coating and assembly capabilities under one roof, supported by AWS and
AI-powered
smart manufacturing systems.
New roles will include CNC operators, welders, powder coating technicians, assemblers, manufacturing engineers, quality assurance specialists, controls engineers and programme managers.
The facility will produce products that power Amazon's fulfilment and robotics network across North America and is expected to launch by 2028.
The investment builds on nearly two decades of Amazon activity in Indiana, where the company has invested more than US$40bn since 2008.
Amazon has invested more than US$230bn in US manufacturing goods and equipment since 2010, while manufacturing more than one million robots domestically.
robots are now deployed
across more than 300 facilities across the globe.
This facility represents a significant investment in the Indianapolis community.

Strengthening supply chains through robotics

In 2025, Ocado Group announced that it would manufacture and deploy
its own proprietary robotics systems
, such as its On-Grid Robotic Pick arms and autonomous mobile robots.
Robotics and automation
have become central to that strategy because of the measurable returns they deliver.
McKinsey research on AI-enabled distribution operations found reductions of 20 to 30% in inventory levels, 5 to 20% in logistics costs and 5 to 15% in procurement spend among companies that have embedded AI and automation into their supply chain workflows.

Amazon is a global technology leader dominating e-commerce and cloud computing. The company continuously drives supply chain innovation through proprietary robotics, AI-driven fulfilment systems, and autonomous infrastructure to maximise operational efficiency and delivery speed.

Headquarters: Hertfordshire, UK
CEO: Tim Steiner
Ocado Group is a British technology pioneer specialising in automated logistics and grocery fulfilment. The company designs, builds, and licenses proprietary robotics and software platforms globally, transforming warehouse operations for major international grocery retailers.

title: Climate Week NYC: Building Resilient Food Supply Chains
content:
Climate Week NYC: Building Resilient Food Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leaders at Climate Week NYC explore the food supply chain. Credit: Unsplash
As ongoing climate events start impacting the food supply chain, leaders from Nestlé, Fair Trade and more convened at the Food Forum at Climate Week NYC
Food is an incredibly important resource, but it is also facing growing risk. Despite its critical nature, it can be overlooked when discussing climate action and the impact of climate change.
At Climate Week New York, senior leaders took to The Food Forum to explore the food supply chain and where businesses can
improve traceability
Speakers took part in a meaningful discussion, looking at where collaboration can make a difference.
A critical period
In recent years, external shocks have made their impact on food supply chains around the world. An increase in
extreme weather events
has put pressure on food production in various ways. Floods and unseasonable rainfall have resulted in food rot, crops have been ruined due to fires and drought and early harvests have been a result of higher temperatures.
The UK Government has declared food security as a national security issue, and other governments around the world are beginning to explore their own strategies.
The food supply chain covers agriculture, manufacturing, storage, distribution, wholesale and retail. As a highly interconnected system, it is incredibly complex, relying on time-sensitive deliveries, temperature-controlled storage, managing supply and demand and picking crops at the exact right time.
Agriculture timelines need to be planned years in advance, but recent weather disturbances have meant crops are ready to harvest earlier than expected, or yields are at a much lower intake. This has led to the growing disruption to food supply chains, with no signs of return to normal production.
As a result, business leaders around the world are looking to strengthen resilience and do their part to minimise environmental impact. Through improving traceability and reducing waste, leaders are working to make a food supply chain that lasts.
Key numbers
The agri-food sector supported 4.1 million jobs across Great Britain in 2025 (National Audit Office)
17% of GHG emissions come from agriculture
UK farmers are preparing for price increases of up to 70%
Nestle now sources 30% of its raw materials from farmers using regenerative agriculture practices
Nestle is committed to sourcing 50% of raw materials from regenerative agriculture practises by 2030
Fair Trade has mobilised more than US$1.4bn directly in fair trade premiums to community development funds in the past 30 years
75% of nitrous oxide emissions comes from agriculture
Responsible farming
The Food Forum at
Climate Week NYC
hosted leaders from a range of organisations over a series of panels. The recurring topics were traceability, expense and governmental policy.
Suzanne Sengelmann, CEO of Lundberg Family Farms, explained that moving to organic or
regenerative organic farming
is a risk for the farmer, as large-scale transitions can take more than three years before they are fully in place. At this time, there is a lack of profitability, as there is no official seal demonstrating these farmers are using these practises. As a result, they are enduring the added costs without seeing the benefit.
“For any farmer trying to start making the transition, it's expensive and a huge risk. So they need capital and they need secured demand,” Suzanne says.
Suzanne Sengelmann, CEO of Lundberg Family Farms
However, conversation on regenerative farming and other sustainable changes continues, exploring the long-term benefits of making this change. Though the initial cost is significantly higher, it is both better for the environment and for establishing long term resilience.
Yann Wyass, Global Head of Public Affairs at Nestlé looks at developing resilience from a global organisation’s perspective. Nestlé sells one billion products a day, around the world, showing the immense scale of the company.
“We are working very hard on regenerative agriculture and there are two main reasons for that,” he explains.
Yann Wyass, Global Head of Public Affairs at Nestlé
“The first reason is for climate resilience, but the second is for business resilience. Fertiliser price hikes, for example, have impacted a lot of farmers recently.
“We are very mindful that the transition from conventional or traditional farming to regenerative agriculture farming is and can be a risk to farmers. So we also combine what we do on Regen Ag with income, living income activities.”
Traceability is key to any claim. If you don't know where your food has come from, any claim you make about it is nonsense.
Chris Ninnes, CEO, Aquaculture Stewardship Council
Policy concerns
Despite this, many consumers and businesses around the world are limited. There are so many external factors which go into determining how people shop, or what they prioritise in their farming.
“You can't just say it's an individual consumer choice because
people's choices are shaped by policy
. They're shaped by how poor they are or the markets they have exposure to, the products that are marketed at them,” explains Paloma Lopez, Chief Sustainability and Communications Officer, North America Bel Group.
“There's no room to blame or shame individuals into making better choices for the planet. Our job is to figure out how we enable those consumer choices that are going to reshape our food production systems.”
Paloma Lopez, Chief Sustainability and Communications Officer, North America Bel Group
The world is currently facing a super El Niño, meaning food security is going to get worse in the approaching years. As a food supply chain is years in the making, the impact is a long-term issue.
This year, vulnerabilities in the food chain have been exposed, unveiling where organisations have dependencies on certain products or processes, or where they have crucial data points missing. The global food supply chain is at a crucial stage, with opportunities to become more domestic and more sustainable.
Traceability is crucial in this step. A leader can only make a positive impact with their supply chain, if they can track their supply chain. Every part needs to be visible, allowing leaders to fully understand their product and its impact.
The forum points to data visibility and technology as a core driver to change, but small organisations are limited without thoughtful policy and large-scale backing.
Climate change impacts
every part of the food system, from the growth of the product, to how it is delivered or the way the consumer receives the product. Resilience in this industry is not just about ensuring quantity, but also nutritional value and diversity of food sources.
Experts switched out on panels at the Food Forum at Climate Week. Credit: Climate Week
Key companies
CEO: Philipp Navratil
HQ: Vevey, Switzerland
Global food and beverage leader with one billion products sold daily worldwide. The company sources 30% of raw materials from regenerative agriculture practices and aims for 50% by 2030, investing in farmer income programs and climate resilience initiatives across global supply chains.
Lundberg Family Farms
CEO: Suzanne Sengelmann
HQ: California, US
Organic rice producer pioneering regenerative agriculture transitions. The family-owned company focuses on supporting farmers through the costly three-year transition period to organic certification, providing both capital and secured demand commitments to reduce financial risk.
Fair Trade
CEO: Felipe Arango
HQ: California, US
Global certification organization mobilizing US$1.4bn in community development funds over 30 years. The organization connects farmers with premium pricing structures and ensures ethical sourcing standards while supporting sustainable agricultural practices and farmer livelihoods.
Aquaculture Stewardship Council
CEO: Chris Ninnes
HQ: Utrecht, Netherlands
Leading certification body for responsible aquaculture. The organization establishes traceability standards across seafood supply chains, ensuring environmental sustainability and social responsibility while enabling transparent claims verification for consumers and businesses.

Automating PUMA’s US distribution

automation with advanced software
Inventory is stored within a compact grid and automatically retrieved by robots, bringing goods directly to employees at workstations for
picking and packing
In 2024, Deloitte surveyed 600 executives from large manufacturing companies with headquarters or operations in the US and 46% of respondents ranked process automation as the first or second priority for investment within the next two years.
Maersk says: “AutoStore helps improve speed, efficiency and workplace productivity while making better use of available warehouse space.

These services include warehousing and distribution, including fulfilment, air freight, customs services and inland transportation.

PUMA's US distribution network
In 2027, Maersk plans to launch its first multi-client AutoStore operations in North America at the Torrance site, utilising excess capacity to process up to 20 million units annually for other brands.
"By combining our logistics network with PUMA's automated infrastructure, we are creating a more flexible and scalable fulfilment model that maximises asset utilisation while reducing total operational costs," says Dave Hune, North America Head of Maersk Contract Logistics.

title: Mars Advances Resilience and Traceability in Supply Chain
content:
Mars Advances Resilience and Traceability in Supply Chain
Prioritise Us
on Google
Mars is working to strengthen resilience in cocoa supply chains. Credit- Mars
Mars invests in traceability and climate-smart agriculture to strengthen cocoa supply chains and support responsible sourcing across global origins
Mars is working to build more
resilient cocoa supply chains
through its Cocoa for Generations strategy, which addresses sourcing standards, climate risk and the distribution of resources across its procurement network.
The company's 2025 Progress Report details investments in traceability systems, agroforestry distribution and supply chain mapping. Mars reports that suppliers sourced a volume of responsibly sourced cocoa equivalent to 98% of what the business required for Mars-branded products in 2025.
The business fell short of its full 2025 responsible sourcing targets but says it continues to fund initiatives designed to address interconnected supply chain challenges. As
Mars looks beyond 2025,
it is placing greater emphasis on professionalising cocoa farming and diversifying where and how cocoa is produced and sourced.
Supply chain traceability standards
Mars' Cocoa for Generations strategy uses third-party verification, farm mapping and supply chain traceability to support responsible production across its procurement network.
All responsibly sourced cocoa is required to be
deforestation and conversion-free
, according to Mars. The Responsibly Sourced Cocoa Programme applies verification processes intended to monitor compliance across the supply chain.
In West Africa, suppliers implemented child labour monitoring and remediation systems for all cocoa volume produced and purchased from participating farmers in 2025. Mars acknowledges that its use of mass balance means cocoa from compliant sources may be mixed with other cocoa during processing, storage and transportation.
The company cannot guarantee the origin of the cocoa in a specific product because of how mass balance functions in its supply chain. This could mean that Mars-branded products contain cocoa from sources outside the verified network, even when the company procures an equivalent volume from compliant suppliers.
"Our progress is important because the challenges facing the cocoa sector are interconnected. Farmer prosperity, productivity, climate resilience, forest protection, community well-being and long-term supply security must be addressed together," says Benjamin Guilbert, Global Senior Vice President, Mars Cocoa Enterprise, in Mars' Cocoa for Generations 2025 progress report.
"Meaningful progress requires collaboration with stakeholders in the cocoa sector, integrated solutions, sustained investment and a commitment to continuous learning and improvement."
Benjamin Guilbert, Global Senior Vice President, Cocoa Enterprise at Mars
Climate risk and tree distribution
Mars funded the distribution of more than five million trees in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana in 2025, supporting efforts to restore damaged land and improve biodiversity across cocoa-growing regions.
These initiatives aim to make cocoa farms more
resilient to climate change
Across Latin America, Mars launched its first climate-smart agriculture programme with suppliers in Ecuador, the Dominican Republic and Peru. The programme helps farmers improve soil health and crop yields while supporting land-use and emissions reduction objectives.
The company is working to expand regenerative farming approaches that can help protect ecosystems and strengthen the productivity of cocoa-growing landscapes. Mars states that its cocoa footprint has been reduced by approximately 1.5 million tonnes of CO₂e compared with its 2015 baseline.
"A global supply chain demands global effort," says Nupur Parikh, Global Senior Director, Cocoa Sustainability, Mars, in the report.
"Through programs that support cocoa farmers in origins across West Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia, we're helping to advance climate-resilient practices, create more economic opportunities and secure the future of cocoa."
Nupur Parikh, Global Senior Director, Cocoa Sustainability, Mars
Cocoa for Generations
To date, 37 cocoa clones have been registered by the Mars Center for Cocoa Science with Brazil’s Ministry of Agriculture.
There were 14 modules available through the Grower Toolkit in 2025, covering four languages.
It’s stated that 28 weeks is the effective period of the lychee-based attractant developed to help monitor cocoa pod borer populations in Southeast Asia.
Approximately 1.5 million tonnes of CO₂e is Mars’ estimated reduction in its cocoa footprint compared with its 2015 baseline.
Technology and procurement improvements
Science, innovation and farmer capability-building form part of Mars' efforts to improve productivity and resilience across its supply chain.
The company has developed improved cocoa planting materials in Brazil and Indonesia, alongside research into disease-resistant varieties. Mars has also developed tools to help farmers identify crop diseases earlier in the production cycle.
Digital initiatives include AI-powered applications designed to detect cocoa diseases and assess bean quality. These tools help farmers and processing facilities identify issues and take corrective action before supply is affected.
Mars is developing integrated pest management approaches and tools that can help farmers prioritise non-chemical interventions, including pruning and the removal of infected cocoa pods. To date, 37 cocoa clones have been registered by the Mars Center for Cocoa Science with Brazil's Ministry of Agriculture.
Programmes like this encourage Mars to "strengthen the cocoa supply chain from the ground up", explains Srikanth Ramachandran, Vice President, Global Cocoa Category, Mars, in the report.
The main goals include "professionalising cocoa farms of all sizes" and ensuring supply chains are more resilient, according to Srikanth. Through its Grower Toolkit, the company is sharing farming knowledge and best practices across cocoa-growing origins.
There were 14 modules available through the Grower Toolkit in 2025, covering four languages. The toolkit supports more informed decisions and the adoption of practices intended to improve agricultural productivity and supply reliability.
It is stated that 28 weeks is the effective period of the lychee-based attractant developed to help monitor cocoa pod borer populations in Southeast Asia. This monitoring tool aims to reduce crop losses and protect supply volumes in the region.
Mars is working to strengthen the cocoa supply chain. Credit: Getty
Meaningful progress requires collaboration with stakeholders in the cocoa sector, integrated solutions, sustained investment and a commitment to continuous learning and improvement.
Benjamin Guilbert, Global Senior Vice President, Mars Cocoa Enterprise
Sourcing diversification and partnerships
Mars' strategy recognises the importance of economic resilience and financial inclusion in cocoa-growing regions, which could affect the stability of its supply base.
Through initiatives such as Women for Change and the Journey to Thrive Programme, the company supports household livelihoods and women's economic participation. These programmes combine agricultural support with community-level interventions, including savings and loans associations and professional farm services.
"Combining the technical knowledge Mars has developed over the years with
ofi's on the ground expertise
is key to enabling precision agriculture practices tailored to the needs of small and medium-sized farmers," explains David Sandoval, Program Coordinator at ofi.
"The Grower Toolkit program has allowed us to share our knowledge in good agricultural practices and sustainability in cocoa, providing the field staff practical tools and recommendations to continue supporting and motivating cocoa farmers to implement more responsible and efficient practices."
Mars intends to focus on professionalising cocoa farming, helping farmers improve productivity, strengthen farm management and build more reliable income streams. This could help stabilise supply volumes and reduce volatility in the procurement network.
The company plans to support the diversification of cocoa production and sourcing through climate-smart and regenerative approaches intended to improve soil health and protect biodiversity. Mars says these efforts are designed to strengthen the resilience of cocoa supply chains and reduce dependence on single-origin sourcing.
Looking forward, Mars is placing emphasis on geographical diversification and improved supply chain transparency. The business continues to
invest in traceability systems
, farmer training and climate adaptation measures across West Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia.
Mars is emphasising geographical diversification. Credit: Mars
Partnering with Mars
Imperial College London
Mars joined Imperial Business Partners to collaborate with researchers on challenges including packaging, recycling, nutrition and agriculture, translating scientific research into practical applications.
Mars Petcare partnered with Calm to explore the relationship between pets and human wellbeing, launching a pet-inspired collection of Sleep Stories, meditations and mindfulness tools.
ADM, Mars Petcare and Royal Canin partnered to support regenerative agriculture across more than 100,000 US acres, incentivising farmers to adopt practices that improve soil health and resilience.
BVA - 2019
Mars Petcare and the British Veterinary Association partnered to explore pet obesity, examining nutrition, human behaviour and healthy body weight through research, awareness and education.
World Food Programme - 2015
Mars and the World Food Programme have collaborated since 2015 to strengthen food safety systems, train smallholder farmers and improve access to safe, nutritious food.
FAO - 2015
Mars and the Food and Agriculture Organization have collaborated since 2015 to strengthen food safety standards, improve mycotoxin management and address emerging food safety threats through science-based approaches.

Prioritise Us

Brian Olney, Senior Vice President of Supply Chain at Wegmans, outlines a US$110m distribution overhaul to boost capacity and streamline operations
Wegmans Food Markets has unveiled a landmark US$110m investment to overhaul its distribution network and scale operational capacity.
The company says its investment will elevate employee working environments and optimise store-level service.
Brian Olney, Senior Vice President of Supply Chain & Food Safety at Wegmans, says: “Modernising our network is essential to continuing to build a safe, more efficient, and more
resilient supply chain
“These investments will give our people the tools and facilities they need to better serve our stores today while creating the capacity to support Wegmans' continued growth for years to come.”
Wegmans Rochester Investment
Wegmans is building a new refrigerated facility in Rochester to support perishable operations
The company will relocate its return centre from Winton Road to a modernised Rochester building
Wegmans' Winton Road distribution centre will be consolidated into its Pottsville, Pennsylvania site
The consolidation is expected to be completed by spring 2027
Winton Road is Wegmans' oldest leased distribution facility, no longer meeting future service needs
Danny Wegman (third generation) serves as chairman, Colleen Wegman (fourth generation) is president and CEO, and Nicole Wegman (fourth generation) is president of Wegmans Brand. Credit: Wegmans
Wegmans Rochester investment
At the heart of the investment is a state-of-the-art refrigerated facility in Rochester, New York.
This specialised hub will manage high-velocity,
temperature-controlled categories
, including fresh produce, meat, seafood, deli and prepared restaurant products.
Alongside this facility upgrade, Wegmans will relocate and modernise its return centre operations site in Rochester.
"Rochester is our hometown and an important part of who we are as a company," says Colleen Wegman, President and CEO of Wegmans
Food Markets
. "By continuing to invest in our stores and facilities here, we're strengthening our operations, creating long-term opportunities for our people, and ensuring Wegmans continues to grow in the community we're proud to call home."
The company is also planning to consolidate its Winton Road general merchandise hub, which is Wegmans’ oldest leased facility.
Wegmans says it will consolidate its Winton Road general merchandise distribution centre to its facility in Pottsville, Pennsylvania by Spring 2027.
Rochester is our hometown and an important part of who we are as a company
Colleen Wegman, President and CEO of Wegmans Food Markets
In-housing grocery fulfilment logistics
Wegmans’ investment in Rochester represents an industrial shift across the

Multiple businesses are aiming to increase control over their end-to-end supply chain systems, due to issues including costs around third party logistics.
According to research by McKinsey & Company, consumer goods and retail businesses that systematically optimise their distribution networks and end-to-end operational planning achieve a 10% to 15% supply chain cost advantage over industry average.
In April 2024, major grocer Ahold Delhaize USA completed a US$480m supply chain transformation to convert its East Coast distribution system into a fully integrated, self-distributed model.

title: Mercedes tests new Gen4 battery cells from ProLogium - electrive.com
content:
Mercedes-Benz is expanding its collaboration with ProLogium and is gaining preferential access to its new Gen4 battery technology. The cells will now be comprehensively tested for their suitability for potential future vehicle applications.
ProLogium is planning to build a cell factory in Dunkirk with up to 44 GWh annual capacity.
Image: ProLogium
The focus is on ProLogium’s so-called Gen4 Superfluidized Inorganic Next-Generation Lithium Ceramic Battery. Mercedes will examine the cells electrically, thermally, and for safety in its own testing facilities, as well as at specialised external institutes.
No decision on series production has been made yet. The tests aim first to determine whether the technology is fundamentally suitable for future Mercedes models. ProLogium claims its Gen4 cells offer high energy density, fast-charging capability, high power output, and strong low-temperature performance. According to the company, the safety architecture includes a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, ceramic separators, and its own active safety concept. However, ProLogium has not disclosed specific figures for energy density or charging power for the cells currently being tested by Mercedes in its latest announcement.
Mercedes and ProLogium have collaborated since 2016. In
, Mercedes invested a high double-digit million euro amount in the Taiwanese battery developer and agreed on joint cell development. Even then, the automaker envisaged the potential use of the technology in selected models. Since then, the cooperation has expanded significantly. According to ProLogium, pouch and prismatic cell formats, as well as bipolar technology, have been tested, among other things. Mercedes remains a strategic investor and is represented by a member on ProLogium’s Board of Directors.
Collaboration dates back to 2016
In parallel, Mercedes is pursuing other development paths for solid-state batteries. As early as
, the company invested in US developer Factorial Energy and also entered into a development cooperation there. The new
testing agreement with ProLogium
is therefore part of a broader technology portfolio and not yet a commitment to a single cell approach.
ProLogium has so far produced its battery cells primarily at its
Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan
. According to the company, it has validated GWh-scale production there and manufactures, among other things, C-samples and cells for demonstration vehicles.
At the same time, ProLogium is also expanding its European production. A Gigafactory is being built in the French city of
, with the first phase designed for an annual capacity of 4 GWh. This capacity is to be achieved gradually by 2030. In the long term, the site is planned to have a capacity of up to 44 GWh.
For Mercedes, the agreement is not only technically interesting but also with a view to a potential European supply chain. If the Gen4 technology proves itself in the tests, ProLogium could prospectively supply cells from its European production. However, the companies have not yet announced a concrete timeline for series production or specific vehicle platforms.
